Transfer rule: If a question asks what a technology “can make,” then test whether any option names a real effect the technology can directly cause, not just a vague outcome.
Error pattern: I chose a broad, colloquial consequence instead of checking for a specific, plausible mechanism tied to the subject.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can I state a concrete causal pathway from the subject to this result in one sentence?” Reject options lacking one.
Use when: This applies to quirky multiple-choice items with humorous distractors where one choice is oddly specific but physically plausible.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for metaphor, opinion, or the “best general description” rather than a literal effect.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a plant “eats,” then map “food” to sugars the plant makes itself via photosynthesis, not to what eats the plant.  
Error pattern: Misread the prompt literally and imported outside facts instead of using the test’s biology convention for plant nourishment.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the organism a plant, and does any option describe self-produced nutrients rather than consuming animals or prepared food?”  
Use when: Relevant for basic life-science multiple choice about plants, producers, nourishment, or food-making.  
Boundary: Ignore when the item is specifically about parasitic/carnivorous plants or asks about what herbivores consume.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which body feature enables a sensory ability, then match the ability to the organ specialized for detecting that stimulus.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping function to anatomy instead of choosing a noticeable but unrelated trait.
Diagnostic check: Identify the sense involved, name the organ that performs it, then verify the option is that organ or an obvious adaptation of it.
Use when: Relevant for animal-attribute questions linking a behavior or capability to a physical feature.
Boundary: Ignore when options concern indirect effects, learned behavior, or multiple traits could plausibly contribute without a primary sensory organ.

Transfer rule: If asked which object is most like a planet’s composition, then compare bulk material makeup, not surface appearance or one abundant ingredient.
Error pattern: I overfocused on a single common substance and ignored overall structure and dominant solid matter.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, name its main constituent(s); pick the one whose bulk is mostly mineral/rock rather than food, liquid, or container contents.
Use when: Relevant in analogy questions about physical composition of natural bodies versus everyday objects.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about surface coverage, habitability, appearance, or a specific layer instead of whole-body composition.

Transfer rule: If a switch energizes a glowing filament in glass, then infer it heats up significantly rather than staying unchanged or becoming colder.
Error pattern: I ignored the basic physical effect of electrical current producing heat and focused on an implausible non-heating state.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does making it glow require energy that would raise temperature?” Eliminate any cold or no-change choices if yes.
Use when: Apply to questions about powered filaments, bulbs, heating elements, or devices where visible glow follows electrical activation.
Boundary: Ignore when the scenario explicitly states cooling technology, deceptive wording, or a nonphysical/fictional mechanism overriding normal heating.

Transfer rule: If an animal-survival statement asks what enables long fasting, then choose the concrete physiological reserve or adaptation over mental state or effort.
Error pattern: Success came from favoring domain-causal biology instead of anthropomorphic traits or motivational wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each option as physical mechanism vs attitude/activity; if only one directly supplies energy or reduces metabolic risk, pick it.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items about endurance, hibernation, starvation, cold climates, or other survival under scarce resources.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets behavior, social cooperation, or a stated exception where mindset/training is the actual mechanism.

Transfer rule: If asked what makes an object electrically insulated, then check whether the exterior surface is nonconductive, regardless of any hidden interior.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on the property that controls contact-based current flow instead of being distracted by internal composition details.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If I touch the outside, is there a continuous conductive path from my contact point?” If no, insulation is plausible.
Use when: Relevant for questions about electrical insulation, safety by touch, coatings, shells, or layered objects with different inside/outside materials.
Boundary: Ignore when the question concerns total bulk conductivity, grounding, internal circuits, or behavior after the outer layer is damaged.

Transfer rule: If choices mix concrete physical objects with abstract ideas, then pick the option that can literally undergo the stated effect in ordinary conditions.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the verb in real-world physical causation instead of metaphorical or impossible interpretations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this be directly altered or harmed by the agent in everyday life?” and eliminate anything abstract, emotional, or cosmic.
Use when: This applies to commonsense multiple-choice items testing literal plausibility of an action, property, or consequence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt signals figurative language, symbolism, jokes, or specialized scientific contexts.

Transfer rule: If a biology item asks what all living organisms are composed of, then choose the option naming fundamental living substance, not foods, habitats, or fluids.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by biological level and rejecting distractors that are merely environmental materials or products.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this term describe a universal component of all living things, rather than something only found around them or in some species?”
Use when: Apply this on basic life-science vocabulary questions about the makeup, structure, or defining substance of organisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about energy sources, habitats, plant-specific tissues, or nonliving objects.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a process during a storm causes, then choose the resulting effect or damage, not the substance involved.
Error pattern: I matched a mentioned material to the prompt instead of identifying the consequence of the described event.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the prompt as “X during Y causes what result?” and verify each option is an outcome, not an agent, object, or unrelated phenomenon.
Use when: Apply this to causation questions about natural processes, especially storms, motion, erosion, or other event-to-effect wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks what the moving substance is, what is present, or which example fits a category.

Transfer rule: If asked what is required for a geologic motion process, then choose the option naming the structural feature that enables movement, not unrelated surface conditions.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering choices by causal necessity rather than association or vivid imagery.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would this process still occur without it?” and eliminate anything not physically required by the mechanism.
Use when: Apply this on Earth science multiple-choice items about causes, requirements, or driving structures behind large-scale natural processes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for effects, examples, locations, or merely common accompaniments rather than prerequisites.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what becomes impossible after disrupting something, then identify the object's real-world function and choose the option tied to that function.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the answer in practical biology rather than entertaining absurd distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the object’s purpose in five words or fewer, then verify only one choice depends on that purpose.
Use when: Apply this to everyday-knowledge multiple-choice items with one sensible causal relation and several impossible or joke options.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is fictional, metaphorical, or provides evidence that normal real-world function does not apply.

Transfer rule: If a safety question asks what you can use directly to observe a hazardous event, then prefer an indirect-viewing method over ordinary viewing gear.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from familiar equipment and ignored the distinction between direct observation and projection-based observation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each choice as direct viewing, indirect projection, or no aid; reject direct-viewing options unless explicitly described as certified safe.
Use when: This applies to questions about observing bright, hazardous, or eye-damaging phenomena where improvised methods may be tested.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly states specialized protective filters or asks about a different hazard than visual exposure.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a resource or technology is related to by origin, then trace the source material or process, not the extraction equipment or platform.
Error pattern: I confused production infrastructure with the substance’s underlying origin category.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate each choice as “source/process/equipment/effect” and reject any option that names machinery when the prompt asks about what something originates from.
Use when: Apply this to items about fuels, energy resources, natural materials, or technologies whose names suggest both a source and a tool.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly asks about devices, mechanisms, or operational components rather than origin.

Transfer rule: If asked what can be renewed, then distinguish renewable natural materials from recyclable or refillable manufactured products.
Error pattern: Confused “renewable resource” with “can be recycled/reused,” overvaluing processing possibilities instead of source regeneration.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Can its source be replenished on a human timescale through ongoing biological growth?” Reject items that only persist through remanufacture or fossil extraction.
Use when: Relevant for science questions contrasting natural resources, animal/plant-derived materials, fuels, and synthetic products.
Boundary: Ignore when the question explicitly asks about recycling, reusability, or renewing a contract, subscription, coating, or product life cycle.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to test a physical property, then choose the option that directly reveals that property with a simple observable effect.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the target property to an immediate measurement rather than picking unrelated everyday actions.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this action produce visible evidence of the property within seconds?” If not, reject it.
Use when: The options are everyday behaviors, and only one creates a direct practical test for moisture, heat, sound, smell, or similar traits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for causes, definitions, long-term outcomes, or when all options are indirect proxies.

Transfer rule: If a survival question asks for hydration without obvious water sources, then consider whether any listed natural item can contain usable moisture inside.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized that “none work” and ignored domain knowledge about water-storing desert organisms.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, scan choices for living plant materials; ask, “Could opening this item release liquid or moist flesh that provides some hydration?”
Use when: Relevant in wilderness-survival, desert-ecology, or practical-resource questions where options include plants, animals, or natural objects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item is clearly inorganic, toxic/unsafe by context, or the question is purely symbolic rather than practical.

Transfer rule: If options mix real natural sources with imaginary or impossible entities, then choose the plausible real-world source.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering by basic world-knowledge plausibility rather than overthinking distractors.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this exist in ordinary reality, and is it a known source or location for the substance?” Eliminate any “no.”
Use when: The question asks where something is found and some choices are fictional, impossible, or biologically implausible.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task involves metaphor, fantasy settings, trick wording, or specialized exceptions beyond everyday knowledge.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a pet animal is likely fed, then match the food to that animal’s natural diet and practical pet-care use.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning comes from everyday biological knowledge plus eliminating foods that are unrealistic, unsafe, or not typical feeder items.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the animal’s class, recall its common prey type, and reject any choice that is too large, processed, or non-nutritive.
Use when: Apply this to common-sense animal-care multiple choice items about diet, habitat, or behavior of familiar pets.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt involves a special medical diet, exotic husbandry exception, or fictional/nonliteral context.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an item’s natural source, then choose the broad real-world producer category, not a material, diagram, or unrelated setting.
Error pattern: Confusing a biological origin question with nearby but non-causal associations; success comes from selecting the generative source class.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this directly produce the item in ordinary life?” Reject anything representational, structural, or merely descriptive.
Use when: The prompt asks where something comes from, especially among mixed choices including living sources, objects, depictions, or places.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is metaphorical, technical, or asks for composition, storage location, or symbolism rather than origin.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is absent when a phenomenon occurs, then identify the condition required to prevent that phenomenon, not the medium enabling it.
Error pattern: Reversed-condition reasoning: choosing what supports the observed event instead of what must be missing for the event to happen.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state both links: “This event needs ___” and “Without ___, this event cannot occur”; choose the absent blocker, not the present enabler.
Use when: Relevant for science items about necessary conditions, opposites, exclusions, or “lacking in/without” wording.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for what is present, increased, caused directly, or most likely associated.

Transfer rule: If a question contrasts two environments for a living thing, then compare basic survival inputs and choose the newly improved resource.
Error pattern: Success came from causal environment-to-needs matching instead of reacting to distractors built from absolute harms.
Diagnostic check: List essentials for the organism—light, air, water, nutrients/soil—and mark which become more available after the move; pick the option matching the gain.
Use when: Apply to simple science MCQs about moving an organism between locations, habitats, or conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the item depends on species-specific exceptions, hidden constraints, or a short-term shock rather than ordinary conditions.

Transfer rule: If a term names a device/material in science, then map it to its core function in the domain, not a everyday meaning of “vehicle.”
Error pattern: Mistook a metaphorical/common-language sense for the technical definition; failed to anchor on subject-specific vocabulary.
Diagnostic check: Replace the key term with its textbook definition, then ask which choice directly matches the thing it permits, carries, or transmits.
Use when: Relevant for elementary science multiple-choice items with familiar words used in specialized technical senses.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is clearly about ordinary transportation, social roles, or nontechnical figurative usage.

Transfer rule: If a phrase pairs an unexpected setting/action with surreal options, then infer the bodily/environmental byproduct most literally associated with it before considering playful distractors.
Error pattern: I overcommitted to a pun-based object association and ignored the direct physical consequence implied by the wording.
Diagnostic check: List the concrete effects of the described situation; choose the option matching an actual secretion, sensation, or environmental result, not a whimsical reward.
Use when: The prompt uses quirky wording, joke-like imagery, or metaphor but still asks what you would “find” during an activity or condition.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly signals pure fantasy, fictional powers, or asks for a symbolic rather than literal outcome.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a raw material becomes after listed industrial processing steps, then map the steps to the common manufactured product made by that pipeline.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a production sequence, not matching isolated words or surface associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the sequence in plain verbs and ask, “What everyday product is typically pulped, formed, and dried this way?”
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items about materials, manufacturing steps, or transformation from natural source to finished good.
Boundary: Ignore this when the steps are metaphorical, fictional, or when several options share the same process and extra clues are required.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how an organism handles short, infrequent resource surges in a harsh habitat, then favor adaptations that capture and retain the resource.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning matched habitat constraints to survival strategy instead of reading playful distractors literally.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: is the environment resource-scarce between events, and does the organism have traits for conserving or storing the resource?
Use when: Apply to biology or ecology items about desert, drought, seasonal rain, feast-or-famine cycles, or specialized survival adaptations.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about immediate behavior, social exchange, or a species known to exploit resources instantly rather than conserve them.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is needed to prepare or use everyday food or objects, then choose the option that is a realistic enabling tool or condition.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the choice in practical world knowledge and filtering out absurd or harmful distractors.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would this normally help achieve the stated task safely and directly in ordinary life?
Use when: Apply this on commonsense multiple-choice items about purposes, ingredients, tools, locations, or conditions for familiar activities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on fictional settings, metaphor, trick wording, or specialized technical procedures over everyday norms.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what has resonating wood, then choose the instrument whose sound is amplified by a wooden body or soundboard, not mainly by metal vibration or an air column.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by the physical resonator rather than by broad instrument family or visible material.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “What part actually vibrates/resonates to project sound: wood body, metal body, or enclosed air?” and eliminate non-wood resonators.
Use when: Relevant for instrument-identification items comparing strings, bells, winds, or mixed-material instruments.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about pitch production, method of play, or modern composite/electronic designs where resonance material is not central.

Transfer rule: If a substance is dissolved in a liquid and the question asks what decreases, then check colligative effects first, especially freezing/thawing behavior.
Error pattern: I focused on a superficial physical property instead of recalling the standard property-change caused by dissolved particles.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does adding a solute change phase-change temperatures more reliably than optical, energetic, or magnetic properties?” If yes, prefer that category.
Use when: This applies to mixtures or solutions where something is added to a liquid and the prompt asks about a decreased property.
Boundary: Ignore this when the additive reacts chemically, changes concentration-dependent optics directly, or the question concerns non-solution-specific effects.

Transfer rule: If an animal trait seems costly or conspicuous, then infer its likely function by asking which nearby organisms it benefits the animal to attract or affect.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a biological feature to survival value instead of choosing human-centered or self-harming distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each option as prey, predator, mate, human, or irrelevant; keep the one that directly improves feeding or reproduction.
Use when: Apply this on animal adaptation questions involving body structures, signals, camouflage, lures, sounds, or lights.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question gives a fictional setting, social symbolism, or explicit evidence that the trait serves a non-survival purpose.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a magnet will stick to, then choose the option made of ferromagnetic metal, not wood, plastic, or food.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by material properties instead of surface shape, size, or everyday usage.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label its likely material; ask “Is this typically iron or steel?” and eliminate anything nonmetal or non-ferromagnetic.
Use when: Apply this on basic physical science items about magnetism, everyday objects, or hidden material composition.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt specifies unusual alloys, coatings, decorative names, or exceptions where the object’s material is explicitly nonmagnetic.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a necessary condition of vision, then choose the option describing light entering the eye, not unrelated events.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the phenomenon to the direct physical requirement instead of distractors about causes, contexts, or side effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What must be true in every seeing case?” Eliminate anything that can fail while seeing still occurs.
Use when: Apply on sensory or basic science multiple-choice items asking for necessary vs sufficient conditions or causal prerequisites.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for a possible cause, an inference about circumstances, or a contingent classroom/example detail.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what belongs to a life-cycle or organic process, then choose a biological/reproductive activity, not a cosmic or mechanical event.
Error pattern: I matched on dramatic “cycle” imagery and ignored the domain cue pointing to living systems.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option by domain—biological, astronomical, industrial, etc.—and keep only choices matching the stem’s domain.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items where one phrase in the stem sets a clear category and distractors come from unrelated fields.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem is metaphorical, interdisciplinary, or explicitly asks for symbolic, poetic, or cross-domain associations.

Transfer rule: If an action compresses an object into a smaller, irregular mass, then choose the term for compression, not shape-changing by bends alone.
Error pattern: Mistook a broad surface-changing action for the more specific mechanism causing volume reduction and crumpling.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does the object mainly get bent along clear lines, spread out, restored, or pressed together into a compact lump?
Use when: Relevant for vocabulary questions about physical transformations, especially when multiple everyday actions seem plausible.
Boundary: Ignore this when the context is metaphorical, multi-step, or asks about the final shape rather than the primary action.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an instrument can observe, then map its scale limit to the options and choose the smallest real physical specimen it can image.
Error pattern: I matched the tool to “physical object” instead of checking whether the object’s size fits the tool’s operating range.
Diagnostic check: Rank all options by observability: nonphysical, whole organisms/large objects, microscopic causes or particles; eliminate anything outside the instrument’s scale.
Use when: The choices mix abstract things, everyday macroscopic items, and tiny biological or material targets for a named scientific device.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about detection method, not size/visibility, or when multiple scales are explicitly supported.

Transfer rule: If a prompt asks what results from losing a basic condition, then pick the option that depends directly and immediately on that condition.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing a nearest causal dependency instead of choosing a distant, unrelated, or multi-step outcome.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does this fail the moment the condition is removed, without extra assumptions?” Keep only immediate failures.
Use when: Apply this on commonsense cause-and-effect questions about missing necessities like light, power, access, visibility, or tools.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for indirect effects, long-term consequences, exceptions, or domain-specific mechanisms beyond everyday causality.

Transfer rule: If choices mix edible items with clearly nonfood materials, then choose the pair made of common foods an animal could actually eat.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering options by basic edibility and typical animal diet instead of surface matching.
Diagnostic check: For each pair, ask: are both items consumable food, and are they plausible for that animal family in everyday settings?
Use when: Apply this on animal-diet multiple choice questions where options include food items alongside objects, materials, or body remains.
Boundary: Ignore this when the animal is a scavenger, has unusual feeding habits, or the question asks about nesting, gnawing, or collecting rather than eating.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where a change can be directly observed across a life cycle, then choose the organism with a clearly visible body-form transformation between stages.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the science term to an observable developmental process instead of picking a familiar animal.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this organism undergo metamorphosis or another obvious stage-to-stage structural change I could visibly track?”
Use when: Apply this on life-cycle, growth, development, metamorphosis, and physical-change questions comparing different animals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about behavior, habitat, reproduction only, or any chemical/internal process not visibly structural.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is likely near a common natural feature, then choose the option that is a direct, ordinary consequence of that feature’s presence.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: matching a basic geographic cause to its nearby environmental effect, instead of picking unrelated hazards or rare associations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this typically occur beside that feature in many regions?” Eliminate choices needing extra special conditions.
Use when: The prompt links one natural feature to another nearby condition, especially in everyday physical geography or earth science.
Boundary: Ignore when the question specifies unusual climates, special ecosystems, or multiple interacting forces beyond the single feature.

Transfer rule: If asked how to increase friction to slow something, then choose the action that creates sustained surface contact opposing motion.
Error pattern: I matched “apply force” with “slow down,” ignoring whether the force actually increases contact resistance rather than changing speed arbitrarily.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it increase rubbing/contact area and duration, or mostly add a new impulse/motion?
Use when: Relevant in everyday-physics multiple choice about friction, slowing, resisting motion, or comparing contact-based actions versus forceful actions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about acceleration direction, momentum transfer, or traction where added force without sustained contact is the key.

Transfer rule: If choices mix inherited physical features with preferences or skills shaped by experience, then pick the experience-shaped one.  
Error pattern: Success came from separating genetic traits from learned behaviors or preferences acquired through environment and exposure.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this usually appear without teaching or experience?” Eliminate those that would.  
Use when: Apply this on biology or heredity questions contrasting body characteristics with tastes, habits, knowledge, or practiced abilities.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question concerns disorders, epigenetic effects, instinctive behaviors, or traits influenced by both genes and environment.

Transfer rule: If choices mix look-alikes with weather examples, then identify the option that is an atmospheric water phenomenon rather than an unrelated object or emission.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by physical substance, not by shape or distance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is it made of condensed water in air? Reject anything that is rock, animals, or combustion byproduct.
Use when: Relevant in science items asking for examples of states of water, clouds, fog, steam, or similar visible sky phenomena.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is about silhouettes, metaphors, or when “vapor” is used non-scientifically.

Transfer rule: If a habitat is described as resource-poor or harsh, then choose the option implying greater effort to obtain necessities, not abundance or ease.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: infer likely survival constraints from environment rather than being distracted by optimistic absolute wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list whether the setting suggests scarcity or plenty, then reject any choice promising easy, quick, or guaranteed access.
Use when: Apply this on ecology, survival, habitat, or adaptation questions linking environmental conditions to feeding difficulty.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt provides explicit support systems, unusual abundance, or asks about a specific species exception.

Transfer rule: If an object is paired with a tool, then choose the action that names the tool’s primary function on that object.
Error pattern: Success came from matching everyday object–instrument relationships instead of overthinking abstract or secondary uses.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What is this device mainly designed to determine or produce?” and reject choices that are side effects or later processes.
Use when: The prompt links a familiar item, container, machine, or instrument with something being done to an object.
Boundary: Ignore this when the context suggests figurative language, specialized jargon, or a nonstandard use of the tool.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what someone might do to alter recognition, then choose the action that changes visible identity markers rather than neutral or revealing behaviors.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the goal to the option’s function, filtering choices by whether they plausibly support the stated purpose.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would this usually make identification harder?” and reject any that leave appearance unchanged or make attention more likely.
Use when: Apply this on common-sense multiple-choice items about purposes, intentions, or practical effects of everyday actions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the setting reverses norms, uses irony, or gives domain-specific constraints that change what counts as effective.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks how seasons change living things, then choose the option describing the typical seasonal life-cycle result, not size increase or unrelated nouns.
Error pattern: Success came from using real-world seasonal causality and checking semantic fit with the full sentence.
Diagnostic check: Replace each option into the sentence and ask: does it form a natural, grammatically fitting seasonal outcome for plants?
Use when: Apply this on vocabulary or context questions about everyday phenomena, life cycles, or changes over time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is figurative, scientific beyond common knowledge, or asks for comparison rather than likely outcome.

Transfer rule: If options include animals from very different habitats, then compare each species’ typical natural depth range before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from habitat-based elimination and selecting by ecological niche rather than by familiarity or body size.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label air, freshwater, sunlit ocean, or deep ocean; choose only an organism specialized for the deepest zone.
Use when: Relevant in multiple-choice questions asking which organism lives deepest, highest, coldest, or otherwise occupies an extreme habitat.
Boundary: Ignore when the question concerns temporary behavior, captivity, life stage changes, or fictional/non-natural settings.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to gain energy after exertion, then prefer an intake/restoration action over another exertion action.
Error pattern: I mixed broad health explanation with answer selection instead of matching the immediate need in the prompt.
Diagnostic check: Classify each option as “adds usable fuel” or “uses more fuel”; choose from the first class when asked about getting energy.
Use when: Relevant for everyday commonsense questions contrasting consuming something with doing more physical activity after fatigue.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about long-term fitness, endurance building, or recovery methods beyond immediate energy.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an element from the periodic table is used to transfer, then check for a property tied to metals conducting electric charge.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a material class to its characteristic physical function rather than chasing unrelated sensory or environmental associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is this option something elemental materials commonly conduct or carry in basic science contexts?”
Use when: Apply this on elementary science items linking periodic-table elements or metals to everyday uses or transfer processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns compounds, biological roles, nonmetal-specific behavior, or specialized technology beyond basic conduction facts.

Transfer rule: If choices vary by intensity of weather or force, then rank them by standard severity and pick the strongest sustained-wind phenomenon.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing category strength rather than getting distracted by mild descriptors or unrelated precipitation terms.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, sort all options from weakest to strongest by expected wind speed; verify the top item is explicitly a wind-driven event.
Use when: Apply this on everyday-science vocabulary questions mixing weather conditions, motion terms, and intensity adjectives.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about likelihood, duration, damage, or a specialized technical definition instead of greatest windiness.

Transfer rule: If a date-based season question appears, then map it to hemisphere using the month and Earth’s axial tilt before considering distractors.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a real-world seasonal model instead of matching words superficially or treating all locations as Earth-like.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is this location on Earth, and if so, which hemisphere has winter near early June?” Reject any non-Earth place lacking standard seasons.
Use when: Relevant for astronomy, geography, or calendar items involving months, solstices, hemispheres, or opposite seasonal timing across Earth.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question defines fictional calendars, non-Earth climate systems, or gives local conditions overriding normal hemisphere-season rules.

Transfer rule: If choices differ by physical state or water content, then pick the one that is a liquid solution likely to undergo boiling.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying options by whether they can meaningfully reach a boiling point under ordinary conditions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: is it primarily liquid, flowable, and water-based enough to produce vapor bubbles when heated?
Use when: Apply this to everyday science questions about phase changes, heating behavior, or which item can boil, melt, or evaporate.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on unusual pressure, special definitions, or substances engineered to decompose before boiling.

Transfer rule: If asked what reduced friction on rocks, then prefer agents that physically abrade and smooth surfaces through repeated contact over agents without meaningful wear effects.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the cause to the mechanism: friction decreases when roughness is worn down by sustained natural motion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking, “Can this repeatedly rub, tumble, or erode rock enough to make it smoother?”
Use when: Relevant for questions about changes in texture, smoothness, erosion, polishing, or friction of natural materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about chemical coatings, lubrication, intentional human treatment, or metaphorical/nonphysical effects.

Transfer rule: If an adaptation changes appearance or coloration, then match it to the opponent’s visual detection ability, not unrelated senses.
Error pattern: Success came from linking the mechanism named in the prompt to the sensory pathway it directly affects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What exact input does this trait alter—sight, sound, smell, or something else?” and eliminate choices outside that input.
Use when: Apply this on biology questions about defenses, signaling, mimicry, hiding, or traits described by how something looks.
Boundary: Ignore this when the trait’s effect is explicitly nonvisual or when the question asks about social preference rather than detection.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives a broad location condition, then choose the option that must contain the process’s usual site, not a merely possible nearby place.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the process to its normal anatomy and rejecting distractors inconsistent with basic body organization.
Diagnostic check: Name the organ(s) where the process typically occurs, then verify which option spatially includes those organ(s) with certainty.
Use when: Apply this on anatomy or location questions that ask where something must be, especially with everyday biological processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the process can occur in multiple regions, the wording is figurative, or options depend on unusual medical cases.

Transfer rule: If choices describe environmental actions, then select the one that reduces waste or pollution through recovery, reuse, or conservation.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing net environmental effects rather than reacting to familiar industrial or disposal terms.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this increase contamination/resource use, or decrease it over time?” Eliminate anything that adds toxins or waste.
Use when: Apply on ecology, sustainability, pollution, recycling, conservation, or human-impact multiple-choice questions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about economic growth, convenience, legality, or a short-term benefit unrelated to environmental health.

Transfer rule: If choices include a body plan specialized for a medium, then pick the organism anatomically adapted to that medium’s movement.
Error pattern: Success came from matching function to built-in physical adaptations rather than surface familiarity or general mobility.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the target medium and verify one option has clear propulsion, streamlining, and control traits for it.
Use when: Apply this on habitat or locomotion questions asking which creature is built for water, air, land, or similar environments.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about learned behavior, temporary tool use, or fictional abilities instead of anatomy.

Transfer rule: If a prompt asks for “an example of” a trait or behavior fitting an organism or thing, then choose the option naming a functional characteristic, not a random category or unrelated similar-sounding word.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the example to its biological/functional role rather than being distracted by vocabulary overlap.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, define each option in 2–4 words and verify only one can complete “is an example of ___” naturally and meaningfully.
Use when: Apply this on vocabulary or science items where a behavior, feature, or trait must be classified.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a cause, external trigger, ownership/action, or non-classification relationship.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what remains after removal or elimination, then choose the state of absence, not a residual property.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the net effect of all stated actions to the object’s existence.
Diagnostic check: Replace each action with its plain consequence, combine them in order, and ask “What is left at the end?”
Use when: Apply this to basic commonsense multiple-choice items about physical processes, state changes, or disappearance after complete removal.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about temporary conditions, partial change, metaphorical wording, or persistence despite transformation.

Transfer rule: If sediment is moving along a flow path, then predict deposition or buildup downstream, not reversal of flow or unrelated side effects.
Error pattern: Mistook a transport clue for a change in flow direction instead of the usual carry-and-settle process.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which option directly follows from particles being carried and then deposited by moving fluid?” Eliminate choices needing impossible reversal or unrelated biology/color change.
Use when: Relevant in earth-science or fluid-transport questions about erosion, sediment, runoff, rivers, or material moving with current.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt gives evidence of unusual forcing, chemistry, organisms, or explicit flow reversal mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If the tool named measures linear dimension, then choose the option describing an object with measurable length, width, or height rather than mass or volume.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a tool to its measurement domain instead of getting distracted by familiar everyday substances.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would this tool produce a distance reading here?” and eliminate anything requiring weight or capacity units.
Use when: A question asks which item best fits a specific measuring instrument or unit-conversion context.
Boundary: Ignore this when the tool is used metaphorically, indirectly, or alongside other devices that change what is being measured.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an animal survives by eating, then choose the option that is a common, plausible prey/food source for that animal in nature.
Error pattern: Success came from applying basic ecological knowledge and rejecting implausible predator-prey relationships.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would this species commonly hunt or feed on this?” and eliminate choices that are unrealistic, rare, or reversed.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items about diets, habitats, or everyday biological relationships among familiar animals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item is about unusual cases, scavenging, captivity, mythology, or intentionally deceptive exceptions.

Transfer rule: If asked for an example in everyday objects, then prefer the option that can plausibly contain the target material, not only a pure textbook specimen.
Error pattern: Overly strict category matching; rejected a valid everyday instance because it was not an idealized or explicit material name.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask “Could this commonly be made of or include the defining material?” and eliminate only choices that physically cannot.
Use when: The options are familiar objects, mixtures, or manufactured items rather than pure substances or precise scientific labels.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly requires pure substances, exact composition, or universally true classification.

Transfer rule: If asked what is used to record images, then choose the object whose primary function is capturing pictures, not powering, calculating, or illuminating.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the task to core device function rather than distracting associated items or brand wording.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Could this directly make and store a photo by itself?” Eliminate anything that is only a component, energy source, or unrelated tool.
Use when: Apply this on basic function-identification questions about tools, devices, or parts in everyday contexts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about causes, accessories, ingredients, or enabling conditions rather than the main recording tool.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for energy that can keep being supplied indefinitely, then choose the option powered by a naturally replenished ongoing source.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by renewability versus fuels that are consumed and must be replaced.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this source get used up with normal use, or is it continuously renewed without refueling?”
Use when: Apply this on appliance, vehicle, or power-source questions contrasting combustible fuels, stored resources, crops, and environmental energy.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about portability, speed, cost, weather limits, or practical performance rather than forever-available energy.

Transfer rule: If a phrase asks what body sense detects something, then choose the direct sensory faculty, not a tool or abstract concept.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering options by semantic type and matching the verb’s implied mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Replace each option in the sentence and ask: is it a bodily sense that can literally perform the action?
Use when: Apply this to vocabulary or commonsense multiple-choice items contrasting concrete functions with instruments, ideas, or category mismatches.
Boundary: Ignore this when the wording is figurative, technical, or specifically asks for a metaphorical, moral, or instrumental interpretation.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what can cook or heat using sunlight, then choose a material/device that reflects or concentrates light onto the target.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the needed physical function to the object’s properties instead of choosing by surface familiarity or food association.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it increase and direct solar energy, or does it absorb weakly, insulate, melt, or spoil? Eliminate anything failing that test.
Use when: Apply this on basic science items about heat transfer, sunlight, cooking, reflection, or selecting the best tool/material for an energy task.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on biology, chemistry, or non-solar heating mechanisms rather than directing radiant energy.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where something naturally occurs “above,” then compare each option to real-world vertical location and choose the physically plausible setting.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the answer in everyday spatial knowledge instead of chasing unusual word associations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can this thing normally exist above the target object in ordinary reality?” Eliminate any that fail.
Use when: Apply this to simple commonsense multiple-choice items about location, orientation, or natural relationships between familiar things.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is metaphorical, fictional, highly technical, or uses “above” to mean earlier in text rather than spatially higher.

Transfer rule: If a seasonal-preparation question asks about surviving colder weather, then choose the adaptation that increases insulation or energy conservation.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the environmental challenge to the body function rather than reacting to unusual or dramatic distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this change plausibly help retain heat or survive cold?” Reject choices that are cosmetic, harmful, or unrelated.
Use when: Apply this on life-science items about animal adaptations, seasonal changes, hibernation, migration, or winter readiness.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about warm seasons, mating displays, disease symptoms, or non-survival traits.

Transfer rule: If asked for a biological source of a food or substance, then choose the living structure that naturally produces it, not an input, toy, or environmental reservoir.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying options by real-world function and excluding things that do not biologically make the substance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask, “Can this thing directly produce the substance in nature?” and reject anything artificial, indirect, or merely supportive.
Use when: This applies to basic science or vocabulary questions contrasting natural producers with nonproducers, tools, or conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about symbolic use, human-made substitutes, or secondary sources rather than natural production.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an animal has produced after hatching or birth, then choose the term for its live young, not the earlier reproductive object or an unrelated species/item.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the life-stage transition and mapping parent animal to offspring category.
Diagnostic check: Identify the parent species, ask “What is the immediate offspring called after development completes?”, then eliminate objects, prior-stage forms, and other species.
Use when: Relevant for basic biology or vocabulary questions about animal reproduction, offspring names, and stage changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is metaphorical, asks about what was laid rather than what emerged, or uses fictional biology.

Transfer rule: If choices compare gravitational pull for imagined bodies, then rank them by mass first; the heaviest object wins regardless of setting.
Error pattern: I focused on a salient but irrelevant cue instead of the governing physical variable.
Diagnostic check: List each option’s creature, estimate relative body mass, and confirm no radius/distance information changes the comparison before answering.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice questions that map everyday objects to physical properties like gravity, weight, or force.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt supplies size, density, distance, or other factors that could outweigh simple mass ranking.

Transfer rule: If an option asks what is guaranteed in a daily cycle, then prefer events caused by regular Earth–sky motion over contingent living or weather events.
Error pattern: I treated common human habits as guarantees and ignored the distinction between frequent and physically periodic.
Diagnostic check: For each event, ask: “Would this still occur every day without any people, animals, or special weather?” Keep only events with a built-in natural cycle.
Use when: Apply this to questions about what must happen within a day, year, or other fixed repeating interval.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt is about probability, local exceptions, or human routines explicitly defined as mandatory.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is easiest to detect after dark, then choose the option that directly increases visibility using external light.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the key condition to the item’s primary function instead of picking something merely useful or noticeable in daytime.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “In darkness, does this become visible without extra illumination, or is it designed to return light to an observer?”
Use when: Apply this on safety, visibility, or search scenarios with low-light conditions and choices serving different practical purposes.
Boundary: Ignore this when detection depends on sound, heat, electronic signals, or when ambient light is absent and reflective materials cannot work.

Transfer rule: If choices compare health or immunity, then pick the one describing impaired immune defense, not generally positive wellness.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping disease susceptibility to immune weakness rather than surface traits like fitness or favorable conditions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option most directly reduces the body’s ability to fight pathogens?” Eliminate any option signaling strong or normal health.
Use when: Apply on biology or health questions about infection risk, susceptibility, resistance, or immune-system function across contrasting person descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about exposure, transmission, treatment, or non-immune causes, where vulnerability is not determined by immune strength alone.

Transfer rule: If asked to identify a learned behavior, then choose the action that depends on training, imitation, or audience/context rather than basic survival or caregiving.
Error pattern: Mistaking instinctive, species-typical parental or newborn behaviors for learned behaviors acquired through experience.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Could an isolated, never-trained animal still do this reliably?” If yes, treat it as innate, not learned.
Use when: Relevant on biology or behavior questions contrasting instinctive actions with behaviors shaped by practice, reinforcement, or human interaction.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question concerns mixed behaviors, reflexes vs maturation, or asks about immediate triggers rather than learnedness.

Transfer rule: If a phase-change question asks what energy drives particle escape from a liquid, then choose the form tied to temperature increase, not a motion descriptor or unrelated phenomenon.  
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the process to the underlying thermal cause rather than to a tempting but less specific scientific term.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option directly raises particle energy via heating, or is it merely another effect, condition, or broad category?”  
Use when: Apply this on basic physical-science items about evaporation, boiling, melting, or particle behavior during temperature-driven changes of state.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for microscopic energy bookkeeping, multiple valid contributors, or advanced thermodynamics terminology.

Transfer rule: If choices mix real emission sources with harmless images or natural elements, then pick the option involving active fuel-burning transportation.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the question to causal mechanism rather than surface familiarity or word association.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does normal use directly release pollutants into air or water?” and eliminate anything that only represents, depicts, or naturally supports ecosystems.
Use when: Apply this on basic environmental-causation multiple choice items contrasting human activities, representations, and natural factors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns indirect lifecycle impacts, trick definitions, or non-pollution harms.

Transfer rule: If a question asks who benefits when predators decrease, then choose the organism most likely to be preyed on often, not the predator itself.
Error pattern: Success came from reasoning about trophic role and vulnerability rather than picking the strongest or most iconic animal.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label it mainly as predator, prey, or apex; eliminate apex predators and favor the common prey species.
Use when: This applies to food-web, survival, population-change, or predator-prey questions involving broad animal categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the change concerns habitat, disease, food shortage, humans, or when options are all at the same trophic level.

Transfer rule: If asked for a learned characteristic, then choose the trait that requires practice or instruction rather than inheritance.
Error pattern: Success came from separating acquired behaviors/skills from genetically influenced physical traits.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could a person develop this after birth through teaching or repetition, even with different genes?”
Use when: Apply on questions contrasting behaviors, abilities, habits, or skills with body features or inherited traits.
Boundary: Ignore when options are all learned, all inherited, or depend mainly on temporary conditions, injury, or disease rather than learning.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which thing produces a biological waste product, then identify which option carries out the relevant life process before rejecting choices.
Error pattern: Overriding the multiple-choice frame with outside critique instead of matching the concept tested within the given options.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this entity perform metabolism or photosynthesis that releases this substance?” and eliminate nonliving or nonfunctional items first.
Use when: Relevant for science items contrasting products of life processes across living vs nonliving choices.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about trick wording, exceptional chemistry, or asks for a literal real-world impossibility rather than the closest valid category.

Transfer rule: If a nature question asks what a decaying or fallen organism may provide, then prefer the option naming an ecological function or habitat outcome over a human emotion.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: choosing concrete ecosystem effects instead of anthropomorphic or sentimental distractors.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Can this directly support other organisms or nutrient cycles?” If yes for one option and others are feelings, choose the ecological one.
Use when: Apply to multiple-choice items about plants, animals, decomposition, habitats, or ecosystem roles with abstract-feeling distractors.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is clearly metaphorical, literary, or asks about symbolism, mood, or human interpretation.

Transfer rule: If a biology item asks what causes overpopulation, then choose the factor that increases births or survival beyond environmental limits, not one that reduces numbers.
Error pattern: Success came from checking causal direction: positive growth drivers versus mortality or regulation drivers.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask, “Would this make the population rise, fall, or stabilize over time?” Eliminate fall/stabilize choices.
Use when: Apply this to ecology questions about population size, carrying capacity, limiting factors, predator effects, or self-regulation.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about consequences of overpopulation, short-term local clustering, or human-defined crowding rather than biological growth.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a biological process produces for an organism’s needs, then map the process to its real-life function and choose the everyday term closest to that function.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a science term into its practical meaning instead of getting distracted by fanciful or unrelated choices.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the process in plain words and ask, “What useful thing does this help the organism obtain or make?”
Use when: Apply this on basic science vocabulary items with one realistic option and several absurd or nonfunctional distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are all plausible technical products and the distinction depends on specific mechanism details.

Transfer rule: If conditions become colder and food scarcer, then choose an adaptive seasonal trait in an animal that actually has that body structure and would benefit from insulation.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning matched environmental change to a plausible biological adaptation while rejecting impossible or irrelevant traits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option for body-part possibility, survival value in that season, and whether it helps conserve heat or obtain resources.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items about seasonal change, animal adaptations, and comparing realistic traits across different organisms.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about behavior, reproduction, plants, or short-term responses unrelated to seasonal survival.

Transfer rule: If choices mix living things with inanimate objects, then pick the option that can biologically consume and use the item as food.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying entities by whether they can metabolize nutrients, rather than matching words superficially.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is it alive, can it eat or absorb this substance, and would nutrients matter to its survival?
Use when: Relevant in commonsense science questions about food, nutrients, feeding, growth, or what something would benefit.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is metaphorical, about nonfood uses, or about substances acting physically rather than nutritionally.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to attract a wild animal, then choose the option that provides a species-appropriate resource or habitat cue safely and directly.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the animal’s natural needs instead of picking human-centered, noisy, or threatening actions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option: does it offer suitable food/shelter, and would it plausibly increase safety rather than stress or repel the animal?
Use when: Apply this on everyday science or common-sense items about animal behavior, habitats, feeders, or ways to encourage wildlife presence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about training, rescue, deterrence, fictional behavior, or species with unusual diets or specialized care needs.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an electric device requires to be fueled or powered, then select the direct electrical supply interface, not combustion-related inputs.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the device’s energy source to its immediate charging mechanism rather than to traditional vehicle fueling habits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this item run on electricity, and which option is the physical way electricity is delivered to it?”
Use when: Apply this on basic vocabulary or commonsense multiple-choice items contrasting electric-powered objects with fuel-powered alternatives.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns electricity generation sources, hybrid systems, or broader upstream energy origins rather than immediate use.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about an animal at a life stage, then verify the anatomy of that stage, not the adult form.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from the typical adult appearance and ignored developmental changes across the life cycle.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, name the juvenile stage explicitly and list its defining physical traits; if the listed trait conflicts with the option, reject that option.
Use when: Apply this on biology items involving babies, larvae, juveniles, metamorphosis, or stage-specific characteristics.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about mature individuals, species-wide constants, or non-biological metaphorical wording.

Transfer rule: If asked what the skeletal system protects, then match major bones to the organs they shield, not nearby body parts.
Error pattern: Chose a local body part by association instead of checking which structure is actually enclosed by bone.
Diagnostic check: Name the relevant bones and ask, “Does a bony cage/cavity surround this item?” If no, reject it.
Use when: Basic anatomy questions ask for a body part or organ protected by the skeleton among several everyday terms.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about support, movement, soft-tissue protection, or special senses rather than direct bony enclosure.

Transfer rule: If asked which item can house many species, then choose the one with diverse microhabitats, shelter, moisture, and surface area.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing ecological carrying capacity, not just whether organisms can live on or in something.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, list how many distinct niches it offers—inside, on top, underneath, food source, moisture retention—and pick the richest.
Use when: Relevant for habitat, ecosystem, biodiversity, or “supports many organisms” questions comparing natural and artificial items.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about a single parasite/commensal host, temporary occupancy, or nonliving factors unrelated to habitat complexity.

Transfer rule: If asked whether a solid is slightly larger than its liquid counterpart, then check whether freezing creates an open crystal lattice that lowers density.  
Error pattern: I relied on familiar material examples instead of comparing particle packing and density change across phase transition.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does the solid float on its own liquid or is the solid less dense after freezing?” If yes, choose expansion-on-freezing.  
Use when: Relevant for solid–liquid size, density, volume, or packing questions about phase changes and unusual freezing behavior.  
Boundary: Ignore when heating, impurities, pressure extremes, porous materials, or non-phase-comparison wording determines size.

Transfer rule: If a prompt defines a condition where a group exceeds local resource limits, then choose the population-growth process causing overshoot, not a resulting harm or endpoint.
Error pattern: Confused a causal ecological concept with one of its consequences; matched surface wording instead of the level of abstraction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as cause, state, or consequence, and select the one naming the mechanism described in the stem.
Use when: Relevant for ecology or population questions about resource limits, carrying capacity, overshoot, or sustainability.
Boundary: Ignore when the question explicitly asks for a symptom, outcome, or mortality effect rather than the underlying population process.

Transfer rule: If two objects of the same material attract each other without obvious glue, static, or gravity effects, then favor a material known for strong self-attraction through magnetism.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying a distinctive physical interaction and matching it to the material class that commonly exhibits it.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Can this material attract another piece of itself in everyday conditions?” Eliminate materials that are typically inert, nonmagnetic, or only weakly interactive.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items about observable properties, especially attraction, repulsion, or other signature material behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore this when attraction could be caused by charge, adhesives, external fields, or when the objects are not specified as the same material.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the state implied by a natural event, then choose the option that matches the most direct physical consequence.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the choice in real-world causality instead of reacting to emotional tone or attractive wording.
Diagnostic check: Restate the event as a simple cause→state sentence and verify that the option names that resulting state without extra assumptions.
Use when: Apply this to everyday-world multiple-choice items about objects, organisms, or processes changing condition after an event.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is figurative, domain-specific, or asks about symbolism, intention, or nonliteral language.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks what an action helps avoid “making excess,” then choose a noun that naturally denotes waste or unwanted byproducts.
Error pattern: Success came from checking collocation and real-world causality instead of matching by topic alone.
Diagnostic check: Replace each option in the sentence and ask: “Do speakers commonly say ‘make excess ___’ here, and does reuse logically reduce it?”
Use when: This applies to everyday-context vocabulary questions where one noun must fit both grammar and practical meaning.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is figurative, domain-specific, or allows playful/impossible nouns by design.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why a place is cooler in sun, then choose the option describing reduction of incoming sunlight.
Error pattern: Success came from linking the everyday effect to the physical mechanism rather than distracting verbs.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option directly changes light reaching skin or ground?”; reject choices that are impossible actions for the object.
Use when: Apply to simple science or commonsense multiple-choice items about shade, temperature, light, or object functions.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is metaphorical, asks about a different cause of cooling, or requires specialized biology beyond basic shading.

Transfer rule: If choices mix disposal and reuse, then pick the one that introduces harmful waste into air, water, or land rather than extending a product’s life.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying actions by environmental impact instead of by whether they merely involve discarded materials.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this action contaminate an ecosystem or reduce waste?” Eliminate any option that reuses, recycles, donates, or repurposes.
Use when: Apply this on basic environmental-science or everyday-life questions contrasting pollution with conservation behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about legality, cost, creativity, or a pollutant source that is indirect or hidden.

Transfer rule: If asked for an indicator of overall size, then choose a measurable extent that scales with the whole object, not a surface trait or one-direction dimension.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the target concept to a comprehensive measurement rather than a descriptive property.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as whole-object measure, single-axis measure, or non-size attribute; keep only whole-object measures.
Use when: This applies to basic science or vocabulary questions asking which property indicates magnitude, amount of space, or overall bulk.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about appearance, material quality, or a specific dimension only.

Transfer rule: If choices mix one biology-plausible response with joke or impossible actions, then select the scientifically plausible adaptation-related option.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering distractors by real-world feasibility and domain knowledge instead of surface wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each choice as biologically possible, impossible, or nonsensical; choose only among the possible ones.
Use when: Relevant for basic science multiple-choice items about how organisms respond to environmental change with obviously unserious distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are all scientifically plausible, metaphorical language is intended, or the topic is not about living systems.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where to perform a heat-dependent task without standard equipment, then choose the option that can supply sustained usable warmth, not just a resting surface.
Error pattern: I matched the object to “where dough can be placed” and ignored the hidden functional requirement of heating.
Diagnostic check: List the task’s physical needs; for each option, test whether it provides them, and reject any choice missing the key mechanism.
Use when: Relevant for commonsense MCQs about substitutes, tools, or locations where success depends on an implicit property like heat, power, pressure, or motion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is only about storage, temporary placement, or appearance rather than accomplishing the process itself.

Transfer rule: If a phrase combines a specific date/time with “leave behind,” then test each option for ordinary, literal plausibility after that moment.
Error pattern: Success came from rejecting abstract or impossible choices and selecting the mundane item that can physically be forgotten.
Diagnostic check: Replace “leave behind” with “forget somewhere after leaving”; if an option becomes a natural everyday statement, keep it; otherwise discard it.
Use when: The prompt is a short riddle or wordplay question mixing temporal wording with a list of concrete and nonconcrete possibilities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question signals metaphor, fantasy-world rules, or asks for emotional/symbolic interpretation rather than literal feasibility.

Transfer rule: If a seasonal-change question appears, then choose the option naming the physical cause, not a later season or unrelated event.
Error pattern: Mistook a temporal association for a causal mechanism; selected what happens around it instead of what produces it.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option directly explain why the season begins via Earth–Sun geometry, or is it just concurrent/afterward?”
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items about seasons, climate timing, celestial cycles, or causes versus correlated natural signs.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for a poetic phrase, common saying, biological cue, or region-specific calendar convention rather than scientific cause.

Transfer rule: If a question asks who transmits an instinct or species behavior, then choose the biological source, not an unrelated object or joke choice.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the concept to inheritance/parental transmission instead of being distracted by absurd distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the prompt as “What living source could plausibly pass this trait on?” and eliminate every nonliving or nonsensical option.
Use when: Apply this on basic biology or common-knowledge multiple choice items mixing one plausible organism-related answer with silly alternatives.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about learned behavior, cultural teaching, or a clearly non-biological mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what enables a sensory organ’s input, then choose the option involving a physical source or carrier of that input.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the sense organ with the required stimulus type instead of getting distracted by unrelated senses.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, name the organ’s needed stimulus in one word, then eliminate every option that cannot physically provide or transmit it.
Use when: Apply this on basic science items about senses, organs, or pathways where choices mix different sensory modalities or abstract phrases.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about interpretation, brain processing, emotions, or metaphorical language rather than stimulus entry.

Transfer rule: If choices contrast fantastical/animal actions with a gradual physical process, then prefer the everyday process that plausibly acts over time.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering for real-world causality and matching the described disappearance to cumulative environmental change.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, eliminate any option requiring unlikely agents; ask, “Could ordinary forces realistically remove this object without direct intent?”
Use when: Apply this on commonsense multiple-choice questions about missing, moved, or altered objects in ordinary outdoor settings.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives explicit evidence of people, animals, or fictional mechanisms being present.

Transfer rule: If a prompt compares seasons across hemispheres, then map by opposite seasons but keep climate descriptors aligned with the actual opposite season.
Error pattern: Replaced the correct seasonal inversion with a same-season weather match, confusing temporal opposition with similar temperature conditions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the counterpart season for the other hemisphere and list one typical weather trait; reject any choice matching the original hemisphere’s season or temperature.
Use when: The question links time of year, season names, or weather patterns between Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Boundary: Ignore this when the comparison is within one hemisphere or depends on local climate exceptions rather than seasonal reversal.

Transfer rule: If asked which material can directly build a basic structure, then choose the option that is a primary structural raw material, not a processed finish or insulation product.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing load-bearing construction inputs from manufactured coverings, coatings, or decorative components.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: could a simple shelter frame or wall be made mainly from this alone without industrial processing?
Use when: Apply this on material-choice questions mixing natural building inputs with finished products or specialty synthetics.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about insulation, cladding, interior finishing, or modern engineered systems rather than basic structural construction.

Transfer rule: If a species declines sharply, then trace which local animals directly rely on it for food and predict hardship for those consumers.
Error pattern: Success came from using food-web dependency instead of choosing anthropomorphic, irrelevant, or habitat-only effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, name one organism that eats the declining species and ask whether its food access would decrease immediately.
Use when: Apply this on ecology questions about die-offs, population changes, predator-prey links, decomposers, or local fauna impacts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about nonliving effects, long-term adaptation, or gives evidence of a stronger indirect effect outweighing diet dependence.

Transfer rule: If asked about weathering, then choose the option showing rock or stone being broken down physically or chemically over time.
