Error pattern: Success came from matching the scientific process category instead of a human action, activity, or unrelated event.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this describe material from Earth’s surface changing into smaller pieces or altered minerals?”
Use when: This applies to basic science questions contrasting geologic processes with everyday actions or temporary conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about erosion, deposition, living behavior, or any change not affecting rock-like material.

Transfer rule: If asked what increases friction on a surface, then choose the feature that increases roughness and interlocking, not appearance or cleanliness.
Error pattern: Success came from using the physical cause of friction—surface irregularities—rather than superficial descriptors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare each option by asking, “Would this create more bumps/grooves that resist sliding?” Keep only those that would.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice questions about friction, traction, sliding resistance, or how surface texture affects motion.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about fluid drag, lubrication, adhesive forces, or factors like load/material not surface texture.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is easiest for heating/cooking, then choose the option that safely conducts heat and is part of normal kitchen equipment.
Error pattern: Success came from matching functional material properties and real-world use, not surface associations or absurd object choices.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: can it tolerate high heat, transfer heat effectively, and plausibly be used to boil food?
Use when: Apply this on everyday-function multiple-choice items involving materials, tools, appliances, or suitability for a physical task.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on wordplay, fictional rules, or nonphysical criteria rather than practical function.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what changing phases alter the appearance of, then choose the object that is itself seen in phases, not a different celestial body.
Error pattern: Replaced the asked-about referent with a related space object instead of matching the phenomenon’s direct visual target.
Diagnostic check: Rephrase as “Phases change how ___ looks from Earth”; test each option and keep only one that yields a natural, literal sentence.
Use when: The item involves astronomy wording, indirect phrasing, or options mixing actual bodies with descriptive labels.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about causes of phases, orbital mechanics, or physical effects on another object.

Transfer rule: If a science item asks what Earth goes around to produce yearly seasonal change, then choose the object at the center of Earth’s annual path.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a school-science fact to orbital motion instead of getting distracted by nearby planets or unrelated bodies.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state: “Earth rotates daily, revolves yearly around one central body; seasons track the year.” If your choice is not that body, reject it.
Use when: Apply this to basic astronomy questions about Earth’s motion, seasons, years, or revolution versus rotation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about day/night, lunar phases, tides, planetary order, or causes involving axial tilt details only.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an environment has “low” of, then compare each option to the environment’s defining conditions and reject ones that are typical or constitutive.
Error pattern: I inverted a core trait and chose something characteristically high instead of identifying the atypical or contradictory item.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Is this usually abundant, defining, or expected there?” Eliminate yes-answers; prefer the rare or context-breaking choice.
Use when: The prompt is about common properties of habitats, settings, categories, or everyday environments and asks for absence, scarcity, or exception.
Boundary: Ignore this when the domain is technical, metaphorical, or asks about hidden mechanisms rather than common world knowledge.

Transfer rule: If a body-part question gives playful nonsense choices, then pick the option matching the organ’s real biological function.
Error pattern: I favored a humorous distractor instead of checking basic science knowledge against all options.
Diagnostic check: Restate the prompt as “This helps with ___”; reject any choice that cannot describe a real physical process taught in basic health/science.
Use when: Short elementary multiple-choice questions ask what a body component does and some answers are obviously silly.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is clearly fictional, metaphorical, or testing wordplay rather than real-world biology.

Transfer rule: If asked which creature travels long distances by instinct, then prefer the one known for seasonal migration over one mainly known for roaming, hibernating, or local movement.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the behavior category precisely rather than choosing by general mobility or size.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option as migratory, territorial/foraging, dormant-season, or limited-range; choose only an option in the first label.
Use when: This applies to multiple-choice items contrasting innate long-range movement with ordinary travel, hunting, dispersal, or winter inactivity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about learned travel, one-time dispersal, habitat range, or movement caused by weather, food shortage, or human disturbance.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a real-world cause of declining soil nutrients, then prefer established agricultural processes over emotional, supernatural, or absurd explanations.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering choices by scientific plausibility and domain knowledge rather than surface familiarity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as natural process, human land-use effect, supernatural claim, or joke; choose only from evidence-based categories.
Use when: Apply this on basic science or agriculture multiple-choice items mixing one textbook mechanism with implausible distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly asks about beliefs, folklore, satire, or non-scientific cultural explanations.

Transfer rule: If choices mix a normal biological response with impossible or fantastical outcomes, then choose the option matching basic life-process effects.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering answers by real-world plant physiology and rejecting absurd distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Would this happen in ordinary plant growth given more of a needed resource, and is it scientifically plausible?”
Use when: Apply this on simple science or commonsense multiple-choice questions about how living things respond to resources or conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question involves exceptions, trick wording, extreme overexposure effects, or specialized scientific mechanisms beyond basic growth.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for camouflage, then choose the example where an organism’s appearance matches its usual surroundings or background objects.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the definition rather than picking a striking color trait without environmental fit.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this blend into the setting enough to reduce detection by predators or prey?”
Use when: Relevant on adaptation questions involving concealment, coloration, mimicry of background, or habitat matching.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the trait is about warning colors, courtship display, temperature regulation, or when the habitat context is missing.

Transfer rule: If a claim says one variable falls but asks what could still make the outcome grow, then choose the factor that can increase the missing driver enough to offset the decline.
Error pattern: Success came from checking causal structure instead of matching surface associations or irrelevant events.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map outcome = unit amount × quantity and test each option for whether it directly raises quantity, rate, or willingness to buy.
Use when: Apply this on everyday economics, word problems, or commonsense causation questions involving sales, revenue, demand, or compensating effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is fixed by definition, all options are noncausal descriptors, or the question asks for certainty rather than possibility.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks what must be produced more because people consume more of a product, then pick the thing that is a primary ingredient or source of that product.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing a basic producer-to-consumer dependency instead of choosing an associated but non-grown accompaniment.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, name the product’s agricultural source and reject choices that are condiments, side items, or downstream add-ons rather than inputs.
Use when: Apply this on everyday commonsense questions about foods, materials, farming, or supply chains linking consumption to what must be grown or made upstream.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is figurative, asks about preferences rather than production, or multiple upstream sources are equally plausible.

Transfer rule: If asked which animal is warm-blooded, then classify each option by major vertebrate group and choose only birds or mammals.
Error pattern: Success came from using broad biological categories instead of surface traits like habitat, skin, or movement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option as mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, or fish; warm-blooded should map only to mammal/bird.
Use when: Apply this on animal-trait questions about body temperature regulation, especially with mixed groups that can seem similar.
Boundary: Ignore this if the question concerns exceptions, temporary metabolic states, or asks about traits other than endothermy.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where a body process happens, then choose the organ system whose core function matches that process.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping function to the correct biological structure instead of being distracted by unrelated everyday objects.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask, “Does this part directly perform the named process in a living body?” Eliminate anything nonliving or nonbiological.
Use when: Apply this on basic science items about body functions, organs, digestion, breathing, circulation, or excretion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is figurative, about plant systems, or asks for a product, cause, or sequence rather than location.

Transfer rule: If a nutrition question asks the best source of a vitamin, then compare options by their natural nutrient content rather than by incidental fortification.
Error pattern: Success came from using domain knowledge about where nutrients originate instead of matching on familiarity or processed-food cues.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does this item naturally contain or directly provide this nutrient in common use?” and eliminate those that usually need enrichment.
Use when: Apply on multiple-choice items about food sources, body-produced nutrients, or products derived from animals versus snacks or prepared foods.
Boundary: Ignore when the question explicitly asks about fortified products, labels, supplements, or regional manufacturing practices.

Transfer rule: If options mix living things with unrelated manufactured items, then choose the one that fits the biological function described.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the setting’s purpose to category membership instead of being distracted by absurd distractors.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option can actually benefit from the stated environment or process in real life?” and eliminate all that cannot.
Use when: A question names a place, tool, or condition with a clear real-world purpose and options span different categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is metaphorical, fictional, or all options plausibly fit the described function.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an analogy about an Earth layer or covering, then map by function and position, choosing the body-part term that acts as an outer layer.
Error pattern: I favored a playful or affective option instead of testing which choice preserves the structural analogy.
Diagnostic check: Restate the prompt as “Soil is to Earth as ___ is to a body,” then eliminate any option that is not a physical outer covering.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items using metaphor, analogy, or figurative science-language comparisons between planet parts and body parts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question seeks literal composition, emotion, wordplay, or a non-layer relationship rather than a surface-covering analogy.

Transfer rule: If asked which object best blocks electric shock, then choose the material with highest electrical resistance among the listed options, not an unlisted ideal insulator.
Error pattern: Replaced the comparison task with an absolute-standard task, rejecting all choices because none matched a perfect example.
Diagnostic check: For each option, classify conductor vs poorer conductor, then rank by how well current is impeded in ordinary conditions.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice questions comparing everyday objects by physical property, especially when all options are imperfect but one is best.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a guaranteed safety device, specialized design details, or conditions where moisture, wiring, or grounding dominate.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an action typically causes to the same object, then choose the option describing the direct physical effect of that action on that object.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the choice in ordinary cause-and-effect about object changes, not word association or extreme alternatives.
Diagnostic check: Restate it as “Doing X to Y makes Y become what?” and verify the selected effect is immediate, plausible, and local to Y.
Use when: Apply this for everyday-world multiple-choice items about simple actions, materials, temperature, damage, or state change.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is metaphorical, domain-specific, intentionally counterintuitive, or asks about indirect effects.

Transfer rule: If options mix ordinary real-world activities with impossible or fantastical ones, then choose the realistic activity that fits the stated condition.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering answers by basic feasibility and everyday plausibility before considering anything else.
Diagnostic check: Mark each option as feasible now, impossible, or irrelevant; if only one is feasible and condition-matching, select it.
Use when: The prompt is a simple common-sense recommendation question with everyday context and some absurd distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is fictional, metaphorical, or asks about imagination, entertainment, or speculative scenarios.

Transfer rule: If a process named in science is driven by circulating fluid or air, then look for an option describing uneven heating or temperature distribution.  
Error pattern: Success came from matching the mechanism to its physical cause instead of choosing surface effects or state-change distractors.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this option create density differences that make material rise and sink?” If no, eliminate it.  
Use when: Apply this on questions about convection, currents, atmosphere, oceans, or heat transfer in fluids and gases.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the process is conduction, radiation, or a non-heat phenomenon where circulation from density change is irrelevant.

Transfer rule: If a biology term names a process, then match it to the organ or structure where that process normally occurs, not to all living parts.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the process to its specialized plant structure and rejecting distractors from unrelated organs, stages, or organisms.
Diagnostic check: Define the process in one sentence, name the tissue or opening that performs it, then confirm only one option contains that structure.
Use when: Relevant for life-science multiple choice asking where a named physiological process happens among mixed plant and animal structures.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about products, exceptions, whole-organism occurrence, or nonstandard contexts like storage organs or experimental conditions.

Transfer rule: If an animal-diet question offers prey categories, then choose the option matching the species’ typical natural food, not an implausible large or human-prepared item.
Error pattern: Rejected obvious impossibilities inconsistently and failed to match the animal with its common prey class.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the animal’s usual diet from memory and eliminate any option that is oversized, plant-specific when the animal is mainly carnivorous, or processed by humans.
Use when: Relevant for basic biology or common-knowledge questions about what an animal eats in nature.
Boundary: Ignore when the question specifies captivity, unusual training, scavenging, or a fictional setting.

Transfer rule: If a definition says a population is very likely to reach zero soon, then choose the status meaning at high risk of extinction, not extinction itself.
Error pattern: I collapsed a future-risk category into the already-happened endpoint by ignoring the timing distinction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does the term describe current absence, or a present condition predicting likely disappearance soon?”
Use when: This applies to classification questions with closely related status terms arranged by severity or time stage.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are not stage-based labels or when the prompt explicitly states the organism is already gone.

Transfer rule: If a question compares the night sky across widely separated months, then predict a changed star pattern or position relative to the horizon.
Error pattern: Success came from using Earth’s orbital motion over seasons instead of assuming the sky stays fixed night to night.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Has Earth moved to a different point in its yearly path between observations?” If yes, expect different visible stars/placements.
Use when: Apply to astronomy items about constellations, seasonal skies, or repeated observations at the same viewing time in different months.
Boundary: Ignore when the interval is very short, the comparison changes only observer location, or the question is about planets, weather, or daylight.

Transfer rule: If a landform is said to be formed by water over a long time, then choose the option describing ongoing movement rather than a phase change.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the causal process type: sustained transport/flow, not temperature-driven or loss-to-air processes.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask, “Does this describe water repeatedly moving through the area and reshaping material over time?” Keep only yes-answers.
Use when: Apply this to geology or erosion questions contrasting motion verbs with state-change verbs.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about weather, the water cycle, chemistry, or short-term physical changes rather than landscape formation.

Transfer rule: If choices mix unreliable correlates with a definitive observational condition, then choose the condition that uniquely entails the event.
Error pattern: Mistook a common accompaniment for a necessary-and-sufficient indicator; relied on typical association instead of logical certainty.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Could this happen while the event has not occurred?” and “Could the event occur without this?” Reject any with either yes.
Use when: Relevant in multiple-choice items asking what lets you know, proves, guarantees, or confirms a state from observable signs.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for what is likely, common, early warning, or merely suggestive rather than conclusive.

Transfer rule: If choices include one ordinary, need-matching item and several harmful or atypical items, then pick the basic necessity rather than overthinking edge cases.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the answer in real-world function instead of getting distracted by superficially similar alternatives.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this directly support the subject’s normal survival or operation without obvious harm? Select the only clear yes.
Use when: The prompt asks what an organism or object would prefer, need, or function best with among mixed plausible and absurd options.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on fictional rules, trick wording, or explicit preferences that override normal needs.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a common factual magnitude, then estimate the real-world scale first and pick the option closest to that typical range.
Error pattern: Successful use of everyday knowledge to reject implausible durations by order of magnitude rather than overthinking wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare each option against a known baseline and eliminate any that are far too large or too small for the event.
Use when: The item tests ordinary factual ranges, durations, sizes, or frequencies with several numerically similar choices.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question depends on a special case, formal definition, or a passage that gives an explicit value.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what tearing changes, then choose the property describing form or look, not state or energy.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying the action as a physical change affecting morphology rather than material category.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “After tearing, is it still the same substance and not warmer or a different phase?” If yes, pick the form-related property.
Use when: The prompt involves cutting, ripping, bending, crushing, or similar everyday physical actions on an object.
Boundary: Ignore this when the action adds/removes heat, changes phase, or triggers a chemical reaction that makes a new substance.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what phase follows a moon phase, then recall the standard lunar sequence rather than choosing by how “big” the moon looks.
Error pattern: Success came from using ordered-cycle knowledge instead of visual intuition or ambiguous everyday terms.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list four consecutive phases starting from the named one and verify the next item in the sequence.
Use when: This applies to astronomy questions about recurring cycles, especially phase order after a named reference point.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question defines custom terminology, asks about appearance at a specific time, or concerns nonsequential moon facts.

Transfer rule: If a hazard is external/environmental, then first ask what body layer or barrier prevents it from reaching internal organs.
Error pattern: Overthinking and rejecting all choices instead of selecting the best available mechanism implied by basic anatomy.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare options by path: source → body surface → internal organs; choose the option that blocks the path earliest.
Use when: Questions ask why internal body parts remain safe despite exposure to weather, chemicals, sunlight, or other outside conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the hazard acts systemically after entry, or when the prompt asks about treatment, immunity, or whole-body physiological effects.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to observe a physical process, then choose the option that enables a real, observable setup using ordinary materials and conditions.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering out impossible, irrelevant, or fantastical choices and selecting the practical experimental method.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option: can it be carried out now, with common materials, and would it directly show the process happening?
Use when: Apply this on basic science multiple-choice items about demonstrations, experiments, observations, or evidence of natural processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about abstract theory, definitions, calculations, or fictional/hypothetical worlds rather than real experiments.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what promotes a body chemical, then match the chemical to its established environmental or physiological trigger rather than to a symbolic association.
Error pattern: Success came from using real-world biology/health knowledge instead of astronomy, mythology, or word-association guessing.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the mechanism in five words or fewer; if you cannot name a plausible trigger-to-chemical link, reconsider the choice.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items about hormones, neurotransmitters, vitamins, or mood effects tied to light, diet, sleep, or bodily processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is clearly metaphorical, fictional, astrological, or asks about cultural symbolism rather than biology.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a simple machine is used for, then identify the machine’s core mechanical action and match the option describing that action most directly.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on the mechanism’s function rather than surface words, context, or broad category descriptions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state in plain words what force or motion changes, then verify one option matches that change without adding unrelated effects.
Use when: Apply this to elementary science items about tools, machines, or devices where choices mix true-looking context with the actual operating principle.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about historical use, safety, materials, or multiple-step systems rather than the device’s basic action.

Transfer rule: If the stem and choices are semantically mismatched or corrupted, then do not answer from the stem alone; first restrict yourself to listed choices and assess item integrity.
Error pattern: I replaced option evaluation with a reflex to echo a familiar term from the prompt, ignoring that the task was malformed.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify that your chosen response exactly matches one option and that at least one option plausibly completes the stem.
Use when: The prompt looks incomplete, contains grammar breaks, or the options seem unrelated to the subject asked about.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is well-formed, the options clearly fit the stem, and normal content knowledge cleanly resolves it.

Transfer rule: If a body symptom is described after heat or fluid loss, then map it to dehydration or impaired replenishment, not fantasy outcomes.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering out impossible joke choices and selecting the only physiologically plausible consequence.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as realistic biology vs impossible/nonmedical; if one survives, choose it.
Use when: Apply this on basic health or common-sense multiple-choice items mixing one real bodily effect with absurd distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when several options are medically plausible, the context is figurative, or the question asks for a mechanism rather than a broad effect.

Transfer rule: If a sentence contrasts an innate quality with another term, then choose the option meaning acquired, learned, or developed.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the antonym/contrast pair rather than being distracted by unrelated or absurd choices.
Diagnostic check: Replace the blank with “learned”; if the sentence reads naturally and preserves the contrast with “innate,” keep that type of answer.
Use when: Apply this to vocabulary-in-context items, definition contrasts, or analogies where one term is inborn and the other is its opposite.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about causes, categories, examples, or when multiple plausible opposites fit without context.

Transfer rule: If a question uses a scientific descriptor, then map the root term to its standard condition or time period before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing domain vocabulary rather than overthinking distractors.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the key term in plain language, then verify one option matches that paraphrase exactly and others do not.
Use when: Apply this to basic knowledge multiple-choice items with one defining word and several loosely related everyday alternatives.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is figurative, context-dependent, or the options require calculation, chronology, or multi-step inference.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what makes something attract magnets, then choose a material-based option tied to magnetic substances, not a property, state, or unrelated ingredient.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering answers by category and selecting the only plausible material cause of magnetism.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option as property, substance, state, or magnetic material; eliminate anything not a material that can cause attraction.
Use when: Apply this on basic science multiple-choice items about causes of magnetic attraction or what objects must contain to be magnetic.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about electromagnets, temporary charging, or advanced exceptions requiring specific elements or mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where an animal lives, then match the species to its natural habitat, not a human dwelling or opposite climate.
Error pattern: Success came from using core world knowledge and eliminating choices that conflict with the animal’s survival needs.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking, “Could this animal normally survive and be found there in the wild?”
Use when: Apply this to basic science or vocabulary items about animals, habitats, climates, and living environments.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is fictional, about captivity, migration, or asks for an unusual exception rather than the typical habitat.

Transfer rule: If choices differ by life exposure time, then favor the one with the least opportunity for physical injury or healing marks.
Error pattern: Successful use of base-rate reasoning from cumulative exposure instead of vivid stereotypes about toughness or activity.
Diagnostic check: Rank each option by total time and circumstances in which skin could be injured, then pick the lowest-exposure case.
Use when: Relevant for everyday-world multiple choice questions about likelihood of wear, damage, aging, or accumulated bodily changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the condition is congenital, medically caused before birth, or the question gives specific contrary evidence.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what chlorophyll does, then choose the option tied to capturing light for photosynthesis.
Error pattern: Success came from linking a biological term to its core function instead of distractors about color change, gas conversion, or debris intake.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the term’s textbook role in one short phrase and verify the option matches that role directly.
Use when: Apply this on basic life-science multiple choice about plant structures, pigments, or photosynthesis functions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is used metaphorically, in advanced biochemistry, or when the question asks about a different plant process.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what lets a climate-sensitive living thing survive harsh seasons, then choose the option that creates a protective growing environment.
Error pattern: Success came from matching functional necessity to the object, not getting distracted by unrelated heat or building words.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it actually shelter and sustain ongoing growth through the season, or is it for another purpose?
Use when: Apply this on commonsense multiple-choice items about survival needs, habitat support, weather protection, or seasonal care.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is metaphorical, historical, or asks about symbolism, exceptions, or nonliteral uses.

Transfer rule: If a word describes a sensory condition, then map it to the core physical property it directly denotes, not a related cause or measurement.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing the literal defining attribute instead of nearby associated concepts.
Diagnostic check: Replace the word with “having a lot of ___”; if only one option forms a natural definition rather than a context clue, choose it.
Use when: The question asks for a basic meaning, synonym, or attribute of a common descriptive word.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is technical, figurative, comparative, or depends on a specific domain context.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how heat passes between bodies, then choose an option involving direct physical contact rather than internal energy intake or fantasy.
Error pattern: I confused producing/storing energy with transferring heat to another object through a mechanism.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it create body-to-body thermal conduction, convection, or radiation right now? Reject anything that only changes metabolism, is impossible, or is irrelevant.
Use when: Apply this on everyday science questions about heat transfer, touch, warmth exchange, or physical mechanisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about gaining calories, long-term warming, chemical energy, or purely figurative language.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the month before or after a seasonal event, then identify the event’s month first and shift exactly one calendar month before choosing.
Error pattern: Temporal-offset error—anchoring on the event itself instead of applying the requested before/after relation.
Diagnostic check: Write “event month = __”; then count one month forward or backward on the calendar and verify the result matches an available option.
Use when: Month-based questions involve solstices, equinoxes, holidays, or any fixed annual date with relative wording like before, after, next, or previous.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for the event’s own month or uses non-calendar intervals rather than month shifts.

Transfer rule: If a science item asks for an example, then classify each option by whether it contains the defining mechanism or component, not by whether it merely sounds active or physical.
Error pattern: I overrode the multiple-choice frame, rejected the set, and answered from general knowledge instead of choosing the best listed example.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does this device use electric current to create magnetism in normal operation?” and select the strongest yes among the choices.
Use when: Apply this on elementary science questions that ask for examples of devices, materials, or phenomena from a provided list.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is open-ended, definitions are disputed, or the item is about metaphorical rather than physical examples.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where an organism lives, then match the organism to its real habitat and reject fanciful or human-made settings.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the choice in basic world knowledge instead of being distracted by absurd alternatives.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the noun’s normal environment in plain words and verify only one option fits that environment literally.
Use when: Apply this on simple vocabulary or common-knowledge multiple-choice items about habitats, locations, or categories with joke distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is metaphorical, fictional, trick-based, or requires specialized exceptions beyond everyday knowledge.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why animals shed a body covering, then prefer a biological/environmental function over a daily routine or meal event.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering choices by adaptive survival purpose rather than human-like activities.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this explain shedding as a recurring ecological or physiological adaptation across species?
Use when: The prompt concerns animal behavior, physical traits, seasonal changes, or broad-purpose multiple-choice explanations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about a specific species, a stated exception, or a directly observed one-time event.

Transfer rule: If asked what is necessary to produce a natural animal-made food, then identify the indispensable biological input rather than tools, factories, or harmful substances.
Error pattern: Success came from separating essential raw materials from man-made aids, substitutes, or irrelevant items.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each choice by asking, “Can the product be made without this in the normal natural process?”
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice questions about prerequisites, ingredients, life processes, or how a natural product is formed.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about industrial production methods, artificial substitutes, or unusual human-assisted scenarios.

Transfer rule: If a clue describes a regular yearly cycle, then prefer the option that naturally changes with seasons rather than daily, monthly, or location-based variation.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the time scale in the prompt to the natural cycle of each choice.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does this predictably differ about four times per year for most places?” and eliminate those tied to shorter or unrelated cycles.
Use when: The question is a simple riddle or vocabulary item built on periodic patterns in nature or everyday life.
Boundary: Ignore this when the wording is metaphorical, culture-specific, or the cycle depends on unusual geography.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a historical conservationist would protect, then choose the option featuring natural habitats or wildlife, not human roles, machines, or fantasy.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the person’s known values to the category of answer instead of getting distracted by vivid but irrelevant alternatives.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each choice as nature, human institution, technology, or fiction; select only from the nature class.
Use when: Apply this on social studies or reading items about environmental figures, preservation, parks, wilderness, or stewardship.
Boundary: Ignore this when the person is known for industry, finance, transportation, satire, or when the prompt asks for metaphorical or fictional preferences.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an action on an object causes, then choose the direct physical effect of that action, not unrelated attributes.
Error pattern: Success came from matching cause to immediate mechanism and rejecting decorative, replacement, or opposite-effect choices.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state “action → immediate change” in three words; verify the option names that change and none that require extra events.
Use when: Apply this to everyday causation questions about force, motion, function, or object behavior after an interaction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about symbolism, long-term consequences, or external additions not produced by the stated action.

Transfer rule: If choices mix activities with a resource-saving behavior, then pick the one that directly reduces consumption or waste.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by purpose—distinguishing recreation/chores from actions that preserve resources.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this lower use of materials, energy, or environmental impact?” Eliminate any that merely describe movement or routine tasks.
Use when: Apply this on environmental science, stewardship, sustainability, or vocabulary items asking for an example of conservation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets exercise, household maintenance, or another definition of “conservation” outside resource protection.

Transfer rule: If a condition predictably changes the physical environment, then choose the outcome with the most direct causal link to that condition.
Error pattern: Success came from using everyday causal knowledge instead of being distracted by unrelated or merely possible events.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does the condition naturally make this outcome more likely without extra assumptions?” Eliminate choices needing coincidence or personal preference.
Use when: Apply this on common-sense multiple-choice items about weather, environment, or other real-world cause-and-effect relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on specialized facts, metaphor, jokes, or hidden context rather than ordinary causal likelihood.

Transfer rule: If choices mix pure substances with everyday mixtures, then classify each option as element, compound, or mixture before selecting.
Error pattern: Success came from using composition-based categorization rather than surface familiarity or physical appearance.
Diagnostic check: For every option, ask: “Is it one substance with fixed composition, or several ingredients/components physically combined?” Eliminate the former.
Use when: Apply this on classification questions contrasting elements, compounds, and mixtures or asking for “combined substances.”
Boundary: Ignore this when the task concerns chemical bonding details, phase changes, or examples where all options are mixtures.

Transfer rule: If a trait difference is asked about inheritance, then trace it to relatives in earlier generations who share that trait, not unrelated body parts or impossible causes.
Error pattern: Success comes from using heredity and trait continuity across generations rather than surface-word matching or fanciful exceptions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, reject any choice that changes the trait type, denies basic biology, or explains the trait without inheritance.
Use when: Apply this on basic genetics/evolution questions linking an organism’s visible feature to family history or lineage.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about acquired changes from environment, injury, training, or non-hereditary development.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks what else is negatively impacted besides humans, then choose another living organism plausibly harmed by ingesting contaminants.
Error pattern: I ignored semantic fit and selected a term that repeated or mismatched the sentence’s required category.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option with two filters: “is it alive?” and “can it realistically eat contaminated food and be harmed?”
Use when: This applies to common-sense multiple-choice items about effects, harms, consumers, or biological consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is figurative, technical, or explicitly allows nonliving things to be affected.

Transfer rule: If asked what all members of a broad biological group do, then prefer a universal life-process requirement over specialized behaviors or fictional traits.
Error pattern: Success came from separating essential survival functions from optional actions and rejecting distractors that only fit subsets.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask “Can I name a normal counterexample within the group?”; if yes, eliminate it, then verify the survivor is required for every member.
Use when: The prompt uses absolute words like all, every, always, and the options mix core physiology with niche behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category is narrowly defined, metaphorical, or the domain is non-biological or depends on unusual definitions.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a natural countable growth marker estimates, then map it to elapsed time/age rather than condition or place.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a stable science fact and rejecting distractors that describe temporary states or unrelated attributes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this feature accumulate regularly over years, and would more units usually mean an older specimen?”
Use when: Apply this to biology or earth-science items about layers, rings, bands, or repeated growth records in organisms or materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the marker varies irregularly, measures short-term health, or the prompt asks about environment, cause, or location instead of age.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what natural cycle results from daily sunrise and sunset, then choose the option naming a changing environmental condition those events directly control.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a concrete cause-effect relation in nature instead of being distracted by unrelated activities or long-term processes.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What changes immediately between day and night because of the sun’s position?” and verify the option states that variable, not a behavior.
Use when: Relevant for commonsense multiple-choice items about recurring daily phenomena and direct physical consequences.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt concerns symbolic meaning, indirect social effects, or processes requiring extended timescales.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why a living thing migrated, then choose the option matching a common survival motive, not an extreme or emotionally loaded motive.
Error pattern: Success came from using real-world biology and rejecting distractors that anthropomorphize or exaggerate conditions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each choice with “Is this a typical adaptive reason for movement across species and seasons?”
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items about animal movement, seasonal behavior, habitat shifts, or purpose of relocation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives species-specific evidence that migration serves a rare, non-survival goal.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what happens when a living body cannot maintain conditions needed for basic function, then choose the outcome describing loss of viability, not unrelated behavior.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering choices by biological plausibility and rejecting absurd distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option directly follow from failure of essential life processes, or is it impossible/jokey/noncausal?”
Use when: Apply this to commonsense science items about survival, body function, environmental extremes, or cause-and-effect in living things.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item is figurative, fictional, or requires specialized exceptions beyond everyday biology.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is inflated with gas during use, then choose the item whose normal operation depends on trapped air or gas volume.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping each option to its real-world use and filtering by physical mechanism, not by category or popularity.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Does using this require pumping, blowing, or maintaining internal gas pressure right then?”
Use when: Apply this to everyday-object multiple choice items where the key distinction is a hidden physical property or use-condition.
Boundary: Ignore this when “inflated” is metaphorical, fictional, or when the object is not a tangible item used in ordinary physical play.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a fuel is used for to help with a basic need, then choose the option describing its ordinary practical function, not an absurd or harmful use.
Error pattern: Success came from matching an item's common real-world purpose instead of getting distracted by impossible, unsafe, or irrelevant actions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is this a standard, physically plausible, everyday use of the item?” Eliminate any choice failing that test.
Use when: Apply this to commonsense multiple-choice items about tools, substances, or resources and their likely human uses.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is fictional, metaphorical, technical, or specifically asks about unusual edge-case uses.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what behavior magnetite helps guide, then choose the long-distance orientation/navigation behavior.  
Error pattern: Success came from linking a biological structure to its core function instead of nearby life-cycle processes.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does magnetite provide directional sensing via Earth’s field?” If yes, pick the option involving travel guidance.  
Use when: Relevant for animal-behavior or adaptation questions mentioning magnetite, magnetic sensing, orientation, homing, or seasonal movement.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about temperature dormancy, developmental stage change, or reproduction without any navigation cue.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a small animal eats, then match prey size and typical diet before choosing a broader predator-prey idea.
Error pattern: Overgeneralized from “animal eats animal” without checking ecological plausibility, especially body size and common food sources.
Diagnostic check: Compare each option against three filters: prey smaller than eater, realistically catchable, and commonly documented in basic biology.
Use when: Relevant for elementary animal-diet multiple choice, especially when options mix plausible animals with absurd or oversized prey.
Boundary: Ignore when the species is known for unusual feeding behavior, plant consumption, scavenging, or the question asks about rare exceptions.

Transfer rule: If a statement describes a destructive event happening to a previously living thing, then infer exposure to danger, not a manner-of-death classification unless death is explicitly stated.
Error pattern: Over-inferred a stronger consequence from the wording and replaced a directly supported safety inference with an unsupported death-type judgment.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the minimum facts entailed by the premise and reject any option adding unstated claims about exclusivity, permanence, or cause classification.
Use when: Relevant for verbal-logic multiple choice with conditional wording, event descriptions, and tempting answers that sound plausible but add extra assumptions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the premise explicitly specifies the cause, type, or certainty of death rather than merely indicating danger or damage.

Transfer rule: If your reasoning identifies a real-world concept not written verbatim in the choices, then map it to the closest option text before answering.
Error pattern: Concept-level reasoning was sound, but answer formatting drifted from the provided option wording.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compare your intended concept against every choice and verify your final response repeats one exact option label and text.
Use when: The question is simple commonsense, choices are odd, vague, or low quality, and one option is only approximately phrased.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task allows free-response answers or requires explanation rather than selecting from listed choices.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is necessary to keep living, then choose the option naming a vital biological requirement, not a gross, unusual, or cosmetic action.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing survival essentials from distracting behaviors that may be unpleasant, silly, or appearance-related.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Would loss of this directly stop basic body function in ordinary cases?” Keep only choices passing that test.
Use when: Apply this on simple life-science or common-sense multiple-choice items contrasting necessities with harmless activities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is metaphorical, about law or identity, or depends on rare edge cases rather than ordinary human survival.

Transfer rule: If asked which material insulates electricity, then favor nonmetallic waxy, rubbery, plastic, ceramic, or dry wood substances over metals or power sources.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by material type and electrical conductivity rather than by everyday function or object category.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would free electrons move easily through this material?” Mark conductors for metals, reject energy sources as not insulators, keep poor conductors.
Use when: This fits basic electricity questions listing common objects or materials and asking for conductor versus insulator identification.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when moisture, impurities, coatings, temperature, or specialized semiconducting behavior determines conductivity.

Transfer rule: If an item is being physically carried or relocated, then choose the option with limbs/manipulative ability and plausible terrestrial access.
Error pattern: I matched a loosely related animal instead of checking whether it can realistically transport small objects in that setting.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: can it reach the location, grasp or carry the item, and commonly interact with such objects? Eliminate any failing one test.
Use when: Animal-culprit multiple-choice questions involve moving objects, neighborhood settings, and options with very different habitats or body capabilities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the clue is about sounds, tracks, symbolism, or trick wording rather than literal physical transport.

Transfer rule: If a habitat asks for “safe from predators but likely die,” then prioritize whether the place fails the organism’s basic survival needs before predator presence.
Error pattern: Success came from separating biotic risk from abiotic viability instead of choosing a merely low-predator aquatic setting.
Diagnostic check: List the organism’s nonnegotiable requirements, then eliminate any option missing one; only after that compare predator exposure among the remaining options.
Use when: Apply this to ecology questions contrasting habitat safety, predators, and survival conditions across very different environments.
Boundary: Ignore this when the organism can enter dormancy, has special adaptations, or the question is only about predator abundance, not survival.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what dissolving a familiar substance does to a liquid, then choose the direct observable property that substance commonly imparts.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by matching everyday cause-and-effect, not by guessing temperature or unrelated physical changes.
Diagnostic check: Mentally imagine adding the substance to plain water and list immediate sensory changes; pick the one most specifically linked to that substance.
Use when: The item concerns common household materials mixed into liquids and asks about resulting everyday properties.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on concentration, chemical reaction, heat exchange, or specialized scientific conditions.

Transfer rule: If a biology term asks what a feeding group consumes, then choose the option naming real organic matter from once-living organisms.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a scientific category to its domain and rejecting metaphorical or nonliving distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option: was it ever alive, can animals physically eat it, and does the term belong to ecology?
Use when: Apply this on basic science vocabulary questions with one plausible natural-world answer plus absurd, figurative, or impossible choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is metaphorical, fictional, or from astronomy, poetry, or another non-biological context.

Transfer rule: If choices mix driving hazards with benign weather details, then select the condition that directly reduces vehicle control or visibility.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing operational risk over superficial mention of ordinary outdoor conditions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this meaningfully impair seeing, steering, stopping, or lane judgment for a large vehicle?
Use when: Apply on transportation safety questions contrasting one true hazard against mild or irrelevant environmental descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about comfort, fuel efficiency, legality, or when several options are all genuine hazards.

Transfer rule: If a stem defines a familiar substance by composition, then identify that substance first and choose the option matching its ordinary real-world category.
Error pattern: Jumped from recognition to an unsupported property instead of mapping the identified substance to the listed attribute types.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the substance in plain language, then test each option with “Is this generally true of that substance in everyday science?”
Use when: The prompt gives elemental makeup or structure and the choices are broad properties, categories, or statuses.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about rare isotopes, special conditions, or explicitly technical classifications beyond common usage.

Transfer rule: If tiny liquid drops appear on the inside of a closed surface, then trace them to vapor in nearby air cooling and changing phase on that surface.
Error pattern: Success came from using a phase-change mechanism instead of picking an outside source or unrelated substance by association.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Can the material physically pass through the closed barrier, or is a state change on the surface the only plausible source?”
Use when: Apply this to questions about droplets, fogging, frost, or moisture appearing on sealed windows, walls, containers, or mirrors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the barrier is open/leaking or when the question is about the original external source rather than the immediate formation process.

Transfer rule: If waste is left uncollected, then choose the animal most commonly drawn to food scraps near human buildings.
Error pattern: Success came from matching everyday scavenger behavior to the setting instead of picking a dramatic or unlikely visitor.
Diagnostic check: Ask: which option regularly raids trash, lives around people, and can access a cafeteria area without special conditions?
Use when: Relevant for commonsense multiple-choice questions about likely attractants, habitats, or behaviors around human-generated food waste.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives unusual location clues, seasonal constraints, or species-specific evidence overriding general scavenger expectations.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the period of a familiar recurring process, then map the process to its standard real-world timescale before reading choices.
Error pattern: Success came from retrieving a well-known fact instead of being distracted by other common time units.
Diagnostic check: State the event in your own words, recall its usual duration from memory, then verify only one option matches that duration exactly.
Use when: This applies to basic science or everyday-knowledge multiple choice questions about cycles, durations, or frequencies.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question changes the reference frame, uses fictional settings, or asks about a different motion than the named one.

Transfer rule: If choices include actions affecting nature, then prefer the one that restores habitat or supports organism growth over actions that add toxins, waste, or destruction.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each option by net ecological effect rather than surface familiarity.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does this increase living things or ecosystem health, or does it pollute, remove, or harm them? Eliminate all harm-first options.
Use when: The question asks for a positive environmental or ecosystem impact and options are everyday human actions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about short-term management, controlled disturbance, or indirect benefits requiring specific context.

Transfer rule: If asked which action helps nature, then choose the option that reduces waste or pollution through proper disposal or reuse.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing environmental effects directly and favoring long-term harm reduction over convenience-based actions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this lower toxic release, litter, or resource waste? Eliminate any action that adds contaminants to air, water, or soil.
Use when: Apply this on environmental-impact multiple choice items contrasting responsible waste handling with actions that create pollution.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about social benefits, legality, cost, or when all options involve mixed ecological tradeoffs needing deeper evidence.

Transfer rule: If visibility in a directed light source is asked, then compare how much each item reflects light back versus absorbs or scatters it.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a physical-perception criterion instead of choosing by salience, danger, or vivid descriptive wording.
Diagnostic check: For each option, classify surface behavior as reflective, transparent, translucent, or dark/absorbing; pick the one returning the least light to an observer.
Use when: This fits questions about seeing objects under illumination, especially when choices differ mainly in brightness, sheen, or material.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on camouflage, distance, motion, background contrast, or nonvisual clues rather than direct light return.

Transfer rule: If asked which animal eats only plants, then choose the clearly herbivorous mammal, not an animal with varied or scavenging diets.
Error pattern: I matched on a plausible plant-eater without checking whether it is exclusively plant-eating.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can this animal also eat animals, carrion, or mixed foods?” Eliminate any yes.
Use when: The question asks for an only/always diet category among common animals with potentially mixed feeding habits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item concerns life stage, unusual species exceptions, or habitat rather than standard diet classification.

Transfer rule: If premises describe a warm, bright, active seasonal pattern, then choose the option that directly matches the implied environmental consequence.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by synthesizing multiple cues into one consistent scenario instead of matching a single clue in isolation.
Diagnostic check: List each premise, infer the shared real-world condition they all support, then reject any option contradicting that condition.
Use when: A verbal multiple-choice item gives several descriptive indicators that jointly imply a familiar setting, time, or season.
Boundary: Ignore this when the premises are technical, symbolic, or intentionally nonliteral, where everyday world knowledge may mislead.

Transfer rule: If asked which option stores nourishment in seed form, then choose the organism type that produces seeds, not animals.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by biological group before considering familiar examples or surface associations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this organism make seeds?”; eliminate anything that cannot, then answer from remaining choices.
Use when: This applies to life-science multiple choice contrasting plants with animals, especially questions about seeds, reproduction, or plant structures.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns food storage in bodies, offspring nourishment after birth, or non-seed reproductive forms.

Transfer rule: If a multiple-choice item’s natural completion isn’t listed, then choose only among the provided options by matching the closest in-domain answer type.
Error pattern: Free-generating a plausible answer instead of grounding strictly in the offered choices and task constraints.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify your final answer is an exact option string and ask, “Which listed choice best fits the scenario’s category and object role?”
Use when: The prompt is a cloze-style commonsense question with quirky, noisy, or low-quality answer choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is open-ended, asks for explanation, or permits answers not taken verbatim from options.

Transfer rule: If choices describe people by lifestyle or training, then compare expected physical conditioning from habitual activity, not body size alone.
Error pattern: Success came from using functional fitness cues over appearance-based stereotypes or isolated adjectives.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rank each option by regular exercise level and whether that activity plausibly improves strength/endurance.
Use when: This applies to multiple-choice questions asking who is healthier, fitter, or in better physical condition from brief descriptors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question defines “shape” differently, gives medical metrics, or asks about looks rather than fitness.

Transfer rule: If an animal is escaping by expelling water from its body, then favor species that use jet propulsion through a mantle or siphon.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a distinctive locomotion mechanism, not just general aquatic habitat or predator-prey intuition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option can actively intake and forcefully expel water to move itself?”
Use when: Apply this on biology questions contrasting animals by movement method, anatomy, or specialized escape behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this when the behavior involves passive water release, defense unrelated to locomotion, or multiple listed animals share that mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a material-property question asks why something is magnetic, then check whether the substance contains a ferromagnetic element rather than focusing on appearance, mass, or unrelated metals.
Error pattern: Success came from linking the property to composition, not to superficial traits or commonly mentioned but irrelevant characteristics.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the offered causes and eliminate any that describe only look, size, or weight; keep the one naming the relevant magnetic constituent.
Use when: Apply this on basic science multiple-choice items about physical properties caused by what a material is made of.
Boundary: Ignore this when the property depends mainly on shape, temperature, electric current, treatment, or alloy structure instead of simple ingredient presence.

Transfer rule: If options mix universal biological functions with behaviors some species lack, then choose the function required across all animals.
Error pattern: Success came from screening for true universals instead of relying on common-but-not-necessary everyday observations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, try to name one animal that cannot do it; reject any option failing that counterexample test.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice questions asking what every member of a broad category does, especially in biology or taxonomy.
Boundary: Ignore when the category is narrower, the wording is probabilistic or context-specific, or the trait depends on life stage or environment.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to perceive something more clearly, then choose the action that directly improves access to the relevant sense input.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning came from matching the goal to a practical causal action instead of distracting, irrelevant, or self-defeating actions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking, “Does this immediately increase usable sensory information for the task?”
Use when: Apply this to everyday-function multiple-choice items about improving seeing, hearing, reaching, or understanding through simple physical actions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on specialized facts, hidden constraints, sarcasm, or when several options could plausibly improve the goal.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what makes an electrical device work, then choose the option describing electricity/energy flow, not a physical substance or unrelated force.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the device to its operating mechanism rather than matching vivid but irrelevant everyday imagery.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the device’s required input in plain words and eliminate choices that are materials, weather, or fantasy causes.
Use when: Apply this to basic science multiple-choice items about what powers, activates, or travels through simple electrical systems.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about fuel sources, mechanical motion, or symbolic/metaphorical wording rather than actual operation.

Transfer rule: If choosing a natural part for structural sturdiness, then select the part whose main function is anchoring and load distribution.
Error pattern: Success came from matching form to function instead of picking a visible or decorative feature.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this part primarily stabilize the whole organism against forces like weight, wind, or shifting ground?”
Use when: Apply this on biomimicry, engineering, or analogy questions about making buildings, supports, or foundations stronger.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets aesthetics, reproduction, nutrition, or another non-structural purpose.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what increases a plant’s light energy intake, then choose the change that directly increases light-catching surface or exposure.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting the direct causal mechanism instead of choices that affect growth indirectly or reduce access.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this immediately raise light captured by leaves?” Reject anything that changes water, unrelated inputs, or shading.
Use when: Apply this on basic biology items about photosynthesis, plant energy sources, leaf function, or sunlight capture.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about non-light needs, long-term indirect effects, or unusual contexts where larger surface would not improve light capture.

Transfer rule: If choices mix temporary natural events with lasting habitat-altering human activity, then choose the lasting habitat change as the likely displacer.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing short-lived disturbance from causes that remove shelter, food, or territory.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it merely startle briefly, or does it make the area unusable for an extended time?
Use when: Apply this on animal displacement questions comparing weather/noise against development, land clearing, or construction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about momentary behavior, migration cues, or immediate reactions rather than losing habitat.

Transfer rule: If asked what belongs in curbside recycling, then choose an empty common packaging container and reject adhesives, mixed-material items, and electronics.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by local-bin material category rather than by whether an item seems reusable or merely made of some recyclable substance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: empty package container? accepted material class? no hazardous, electronic, or sticky contamination? Pick only those passing all checks.
Use when: Apply on waste-sorting questions contrasting everyday packaging with personal-care products, repair supplies, gadgets, or other non-container items.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is about specialty drop-off programs, e-waste collection, deposit returns, or location-specific recycling exceptions.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a scientific process causes, then choose the option describing a general physical or chemical change, not a human action or impossible state.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering answers by domain plausibility and mechanism match rather than surface familiarity.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask “Can this directly result from the process in ordinary science?” and reject any option that is animate, irrelevant, or fantastical.
Use when: Apply this on basic science multiple-choice items where one answer reflects realistic effects and distractors are absurd or off-domain.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item is metaphorical, fictional, or requires a highly specific technical exception beyond everyday science.

Transfer rule: If asked for a source of heat, then choose the option that converts stored energy into thermal output during normal use.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by whether they actively generate heat versus merely making surroundings colder.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does this item/process release energy as warmth by itself?” and eliminate choices that only absorb heat or change location.
Use when: Apply this on everyday science questions contrasting devices, actions, or environments by their thermal effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks about indirect warming, long-term metabolism, insulation, or context-specific survival strategies.

Transfer rule: If a place-formation question contrasts mythic agents with geological processes, then default to the specific natural mechanism unless the prompt is explicitly about legend.
Error pattern: Chose a culturally appealing narrative over an evidence-based physical explanation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as folklore, weather event, sudden disaster, or long-term geology; prefer the category that plausibly creates enduring landforms.
Use when: The question asks how a location, landform, or city site was formed and includes both supernatural and natural causes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the source is clearly mythology, religion, oral tradition, or asks for a symbolic/traditional account rather than physical origin.

Transfer rule: If a verb about an organism’s end-of-life state appears, then select the option naming the normal physical post-death process.
Error pattern: Success came from using real-world causality and word meaning, not distractors with positive, reversible, or emotional outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Replace the subject with “a dead body” and ask which option still describes an inevitable, biological change.
Use when: Apply this to commonsense vocabulary questions about life processes, consequences, or states where one option matches natural physical reality.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is figurative, legal, technical, or context changes the meaning away from literal biology.

Transfer rule: If a prompt links very early darkness or abruptly shorter daylight to a likely condition, then favor cold-season implications over celebratory or summer-related events.
Error pattern: I matched a keyword about daylight to a memorable calendar event instead of checking the underlying seasonal direction implied by faster nightfall.
Diagnostic check: Translate the clue into a physical trend: “days are shortening?” If yes, ask which options fit colder, later-in-year conditions and reject those tied to longer days.
Use when: This applies to commonsense multiple-choice items about seasons, weather, daylight length, or time-of-year cues.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt mentions unusual geography, artificial lighting, exact holidays, or a metaphorical use of day/night.

Transfer rule: If one option is a real seasonal event tied to daylight/cold, then choose it over joke or daily-routine distractors.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the phrase in basic world knowledge and rejecting absurd choices rather than overthinking wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as natural phenomenon, human activity, or nonsense; prefer the only category that can plausibly affect plant life cycles.
Use when: Apply this on common-sense multiple-choice items about biology, seasons, weather, or everyday phenomena with humorous distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when several realistic scientific options exist and the task requires finer domain knowledge, definitions, or exceptions.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an adaptation humans created with science, then choose a science-enabled capability or tool-assisted function, not an innate body trait or biological byproduct.
Error pattern: Confusing natural human characteristics with externally engineered adaptations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would humans have this without technology or deliberate invention?” Eliminate any option answered yes.
Use when: The prompt contrasts biological features against abilities made possible by inventions, engineering, or applied science.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about evolved traits, inherited variation, or adaptations in the biological sense.

Transfer rule: If an object’s main function depends on changing temperature, then choose the option describing the produced condition that enables that function.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping tool purpose to its direct physical output instead of matching words by association alone.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What does this item actively generate during normal use?” then reject options describing the opposite state or impossible byproducts.
Use when: Apply this to everyday-function multiple-choice questions about appliances, tools, or devices with a primary physical effect.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns unusual failures, metaphorical uses, or secondary outcomes rather than normal operation.

Transfer rule: If a date-based seasons question involves June or December, then first map it to hemisphere before evaluating choices.  
Error pattern: I applied one hemisphere’s calendar globally and chose a joke option instead of checking the opposite hemisphere.  
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which hemisphere has shortest daylight on this date?” Then verify that one realistic geography option matches that hemisphere.  
Use when: The prompt mentions solstice/equinox, daylight length, seasons, or a calendar date tied to Earth regions or hemispheres.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is fictional, non-Earth, or defines seasons by a special local convention.

Transfer rule: If a question links a common substance to a sensory food effect, then map it to its well-known taste quality rather than texture or temperature.
Error pattern: Success came from using basic real-world semantic knowledge about ingredients and taste associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as taste, texture, temperature, or unrelated; choose only one matching the substance’s typical flavor effect.
Use when: Apply this to everyday knowledge multiple-choice items about foods, ingredients, senses, or familiar material properties.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt specifies an unusual context, metaphorical usage, chemistry beyond common experience, or asks about non-sensory effects.

Transfer rule: If choices mix everyday actions with a bodily process, then select the one directly involved in producing or enabling offspring, not just any life activity.
Error pattern: I applied broad world knowledge and rejected all options instead of choosing the best fit among imperfect or oddly phrased choices.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this process affect gametes, fertilization, pregnancy, or release of reproductive material?” Pick the only yes.
Use when: This is relevant on basic biology multiple choice items with awkward wording, misspellings, or distractors that are ordinary behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a precise textbook definition or when multiple options clearly involve reproductive processes.
